cau_hoi: In which country is the Great Wall located?
giai_thich: The Great Wall was built and extended by many Chinese dynasties over more than 2000 years to prevent nomadic tribes from the North. The most beautiful sections that visitors see today were mainly constructed during the Ming Dynasty. The total length of the wall segments reaches over 20,000 km. Contrary to popular belief, it cannot be seen with the naked eye from the Moon.

cau_hoi: In which country is the Taj Mahal located?
giai_thich: The Taj Mahal in Agra, India, was commissioned by Mughal Emperor Shah Jahan in memory of his beloved wife Mumtaz Mahal. About 20,000 workers labored for approximately 20 years (1632 – 1653). The white marble mausoleum changes color with the light: pink in the morning, white at noon, and yellow under the moon.

cau_hoi: What are the Japanese feudal warriors, who carry katana swords, called?
giai_thich: Samurai were the warrior class serving the feudal lords, living by a code of honor known as Bushido. The shogun was the general who led the samurai, while ninjas were spies and assassins operating in secrecy. In 1876, the Meiji government banned samurai from wearing swords in public, marking the end of their era.

cau_hoi: Which empire was founded by Genghis Khan?
giai_thich: In 1206, Genghis Khan united the tribes on the Mongolian steppe. He and his descendants established the Mongol Empire, which had the largest contiguous territory in history, stretching from Korea to Poland. His secret was an extremely mobile cavalry and a system of relay stations for communication throughout the empire.

cau_hoi: In which country is the Angkor Wat temple complex located?
giai_thich: Angkor Wat was built by the Khmer Empire in the 12th century, originally dedicated to the Hindu god Vishnu, and later became a Buddhist temple. It is the largest religious monument in the world. Angkor Wat is so important to the Cambodian people that the temple's image appears on the national flag.

cau_hoi: Which leader led the independence movement for which country?
giai_thich: Gandhi led the Indian people against British rule through nonviolent methods: peaceful protests, boycotting British goods, and fasting. "Mahatma" is not his real name but a title meaning "Great Soul." India gained independence in 1947, and his birthday (October 2) is now observed as International Day of Non-Violence.

cau_hoi: What was the first Japanese city to be bombed with an atomic bomb in 1945?
giai_thich: On August 6, 1945, an American plane dropped the atomic bomb "Little Boy" on Hiroshima, killing approximately 70,000 – 80,000 people instantly. Three days later, a second bomb fell on Nagasaki. Today, the Hiroshima Peace Memorial Park reminds the world of the horrors of nuclear weapons.

cau_hoi: What is the name of the ancient trade route that connected China to Europe, famous for silk?
giai_thich: The Silk Road was actually a network of many overland routes through Central Asia, active since the Han Dynasty. Besides silk, goods exchanged included paper, ceramics, spices, horses, and even religions like Buddhism. The name "Silk Road" was coined by German geographer Ferdinand von Richthofen in 1877.

cau_hoi: Which Italian traveler recounted his journey to China during the Yuan Dynasty?
giai_thich: Marco Polo, a Venetian, arrived in China around 1275 and served under Kublai Khan for about 17 years. Upon returning home, he was imprisoned and told his stories to a fellow prisoner who transcribed them into the book "The Travels of Marco Polo." This book later inspired Columbus to seek a route to Asia.

cau_hoi: In which city is the Forbidden City, the palace of Chinese emperors, located?
giai_thich: The Forbidden City was built in the early 15th century during the Ming Dynasty and was home to 24 emperors of the Ming and Qing dynasties. It is called the "Forbidden City" because commoners were not allowed to enter. The complex consists of about 980 buildings and is now the Palace Museum.

cau_hoi: What was the title of the general who truly held power in feudal Japan?
giai_thich: For about 700 years (1192 – 1867), the Emperor held only a symbolic role in Kyoto, while the Shogun (general) commanded the military and government. Daimyos were local lords who had to obey the Shogun. The Shogunate ended when power was returned to Emperor Meiji in 1868.

cau_hoi: Which country in Southeast Asia has never been colonized by the West?
giai_thich: Siam (Thailand) maintained its independence thanks to skillful diplomacy by its kings, modernizing the country and ceding some territories to Britain and France. Thailand also served as a "buffer zone" between British-controlled Myanmar and French Indochina. Myanmar and Malaysia were once British colonies, while Indonesia was formerly Dutch.

cau_hoi: In 1945, Japan was bombed with atomic bombs in Hiroshima and which city?
giai_thich: On August 9, 1945, the "Fat Man" bomb was dropped on Nagasaki. The original target was the city of Kokura, but due to cloudy weather, the plane diverted. Kyoto was on the target list but was removed due to its cultural significance. On August 15, 1945, Japan announced its surrender.

cau_hoi: On December 7, 1941, Japan unexpectedly attacked which U.S. naval base?
giai_thich: Aircraft from six Japanese aircraft carriers attacked Pearl Harbor in Hawaii, sinking or damaging many battleships and killing about 2,400 Americans. President Roosevelt called it "a date which will live in infamy." The next day, the U.S. declared war on Japan and officially entered World War II.

cau_hoi: When did India gain independence from Britain?
giai_thich: On August 15, 1947, India became an independent nation, and British India was divided into two countries, India and Pakistan. Prime Minister Nehru delivered his famous "Tryst with Destiny" speech at midnight. The year 1950 marked the enactment of the Indian Constitution, making India a republic.

cau_hoi: What was the last feudal dynasty of China?
giai_thich: The Qing Dynasty, established by the Manchus, ruled China from 1644 to 1912. By the end of the Qing era, China lost many wars against the West and Japan. The Xinhai Revolution in 1911 overthrew the Qing, ending over 2000 years of monarchy in China.

cau_hoi: When did Britain hand Hong Kong back to China?
giai_thich: Hong Kong was under British control after the Opium Wars. Most of the territory (New Territories) was leased to Britain for 99 years starting in 1898, so the lease expired in 1997. On July 1, 1997, Hong Kong was returned to China under the principle of "one country, two systems." The year 1984 was when the two countries signed a joint declaration on the handover, while 1999 was when Macau was returned.

cau_hoi: Who declared the establishment of the People's Republic of China in 1949?
giai_thich: On October 1, 1949, Mao Zedong declared the establishment of the People's Republic of China from the Tiananmen Gate, after the Communist Party defeated the Kuomintang in the civil war. Chiang Kai-shek retreated to Taiwan. October 1 is now celebrated as China's National Day.

cau_hoi: What religion did the royal family of the Mughal Empire in India follow?
giai_thich: The Mughal emperors were descendants of Genghis Khan and Timur, following Islam, ruling over most of the Indian subcontinent where the majority of the population practiced Hinduism. The term "Mughal" is derived from the Persian word for "Mongol." They left behind many famous structures such as the Taj Mahal and the Red Fort.

cau_hoi: Which country in Asia was a Dutch colony for many centuries?
giai_thich: From the early 17th century, the Dutch East India Company (VOC) gradually controlled the islands of Indonesia to trade spices such as cloves and nutmeg. After 1800, the Dutch government directly ruled the region under the name Dutch East Indies. The Philippines was once a Spanish and then American colony, while Malaysia and Myanmar were British colonies.

cau_hoi: Which king is the Philippines named after?
giai_thich: In 1543, explorer Ruy López de Villalobos named several islands "Las Islas Filipinas" in honor of Prince Philip, who later became King Philip II. The Philippines was a Spanish colony for over 300 years, which is why most of the population is Catholic, a rarity in Asia.

cau_hoi: When did the Korean War begin?
giai_thich: On June 25, 1950, North Korean troops crossed the 38th parallel and moved south. The United Nations, led by the United States, sided with South Korea, while China sent troops to support North Korea. In 1953, both sides signed an armistice agreement, but there has still been no official peace treaty.

cau_hoi: The Opium War broke out between the Qing Dynasty and which country?
giai_thich: British merchants sold opium from India to China, leading to millions of addicts and silver flowing out of the country. When the Qing Dynasty banned and destroyed opium, Britain went to war (1839 – 1842) and won thanks to modern warships. The Second Opium War (1856 – 1860) saw France join in.

cau_hoi: Before moving to Tokyo during the Meiji era, where was the capital of the Japanese Emperor?
giai_thich: Kyoto was the capital of the Emperor for over 1000 years, from 794 to 1868. During the Meiji era, the Emperor moved to Edo and renamed it Tokyo, meaning "Eastern Capital." In Japanese, the word "Kyoto" simply means "capital." Nara was the capital before Kyoto, while Kamakura was the land of the first shogunate.

cau_hoi: According to the Treaty of Nanking in 1842, which island did the Qing Dynasty have to cede to Britain?
giai_thich: The Treaty of Nanking ended the First Opium War. This was the first "unequal treaty": China had to permanently cede Hong Kong, open 5 ports for British trade, and pay war reparations. At that time, Hong Kong was just a sparsely populated rock island, which later became one of the world's largest financial centers.

cau_hoi: Which country was Macau formerly a colony of?
giai_thich: The Portuguese were allowed to settle in Macau from 1557 for trade, and it was the first and last European colony in China. Macau was handed back to China on December 20, 1999, two years after Hong Kong. Today, Macau is famous for its architecture that blends Portuguese and Chinese styles.

cau_hoi: Who was the first Prime Minister of Singapore, regarded as the builder of modern Singapore?
giai_thich: Lee Kuan Yew served as Prime Minister from 1959 to 1990. When Singapore gained independence in 1965, it was a small island with no resources. He focused on education, anti-corruption, and attracting investment, transforming Singapore into one of the richest countries in the world. Stamford Raffles was the British who established the Singapore trading post in 1819.

cau_hoi: When did the Meiji Restoration period begin in Japan?
giai_thich: In 1868, power was restored to Emperor Meiji, ending the shogunate. Japan sent people to the West to learn, built railways, factories, a modern military, and a school system. In just about 40 years, Japan became a power capable of defeating Russia in 1905. The year 1853 was when American ships arrived to force Japan to open up.

cau_hoi: Who was the last emperor of China?
giai_thich: Puyi ascended the throne in 1908 at nearly 3 years old and had to abdicate in 1912 after the Xinhai Revolution. Later, Japan made him a puppet emperor of Manchukuo. In his later life, he lived as an ordinary citizen in Beijing, working at the botanical garden. His life was depicted in the film "The Last Emperor" (1987).

cau_hoi: Sun Yat-sen was the leader of which revolution in 1911 that overthrew the Qing Dynasty?
giai_thich: The Xinhai Revolution (1911 is the year of Xinhai according to the lunar calendar) overthrew the Qing Dynasty and established the Republic of China, the first republican state in Asia. Sun Yat-sen proposed the "Three Principles of the People": nationalism, democracy, and people's livelihood. He is revered as the "Father of the Nation" in both mainland China and Taiwan.

cau_hoi: Which Korean king created the Hangul alphabet in the 15th century?
giai_thich: Previously, Koreans used Hanja, which was very difficult for common people to learn. In 1443, King Sejong and scholars created the Hangul alphabet, announced in 1446, with letters mimicking the shape of the mouth and tongue when pronounced. It is said that intelligent people can learn Hangul in a morning. October 9 is Hangul Day in South Korea.

cau_hoi: Which port city was the center of a powerful Islamic kingdom and was captured by the Portuguese in 1511?
giai_thich: Malacca is located on the strait of the same name, the shortest sea route connecting the Indian Ocean with the South China Sea. In the 15th century, it was one of the busiest spice trading ports in Asia. In 1511, Afonso de Albuquerque captured Malacca for Portugal. The city later came under Dutch and then British control.

cau_hoi: Pakistan separated from British India in 1947 primarily based on which factor?
giai_thich: The Muslim League was concerned that Muslims would be marginalized in a predominantly Hindu India, thus demanding a separate nation. Pakistan was established from regions with a Muslim majority in the northwest and east. The partition led to about 15 million people migrating and hundreds of thousands dying in riots.

cau_hoi: In 1971, which country did East Pakistan become independent?
giai_thich: Pakistan originally consisted of two parts separated by about 1,600 km through Indian territory. The people of East Pakistan spoke Bengali and were dissatisfied with the oppression from the west. After the war in 1971, supported by India, Bangladesh was born. The name means 'Land of the Bengalis.'

cau_hoi: In which city was the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) founded in 1967?
giai_thich: On August 8, 1967, the foreign ministers of five countries—Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines, Singapore, and Thailand—signed the Bangkok Declaration, establishing ASEAN. Today, ASEAN has 11 members after East Timor joined. Vietnam joined ASEAN in 1995. The ASEAN Secretariat is located in Jakarta, which can lead to confusion.

cau_hoi: The two Mongol fleets that attacked Japan both failed due to storms. What did the Japanese call those storms?
giai_thich: In 1274 and 1281, Emperor Kublai Khan sent large fleets to Japan, but both times they were destroyed by storms. The Japanese believed that the gods sent 'divine winds' (kamikaze) to protect the country. During World War II, this name was used for pilots who carried out suicide attacks by crashing planes into enemy ships.

cau_hoi: Which Ming admiral commanded seven major voyages to the Indian Ocean in the early 15th century?
giai_thich: From 1405 to 1433, Zheng He led enormous fleets, sometimes with over 300 ships and around 27,000 people, to Southeast Asia, India, Arabia, and East Africa. He even brought giraffes from Africa back to the court. After his death, the Ming dynasty ceased maritime expeditions and closed itself off from the world.

cau_hoi: In 1853, which American admiral led the 'black ships' to force Japan to open up?
giai_thich: Admiral Matthew Perry brought four black-painted warships, including steam-powered vessels, into Edo Bay and demanded that Japan open its ports for trade. The following year, he returned with more ships, and Japan had to sign the Treaty of Kanagawa. This event weakened the shogunate and led to the Meiji Restoration. MacArthur was the general who occupied Japan after 1945.

cau_hoi: Which Mughal emperor commissioned the construction of the Taj Mahal?
giai_thich: Shah Jahan commissioned the Taj Mahal after his wife Mumtaz Mahal died in 1631 while giving birth to their 14th child. He also built the Red Fort in Delhi. In his later years, he was imprisoned by his own son Aurangzeb in the Agra Fort, where he could only view the Taj Mahal from a distance. After his death, he was buried next to his wife in the mausoleum.

cau_hoi: Who founded the Mughal Empire in 1526?
giai_thich: Babur was a descendant of Timur (on his mother's side) and Genghis Khan (on his father's side). He descended from Central Asia into India and won the Battle of Panipat in 1526 using guns and cannons. Babur also wrote the memoir 'Baburnama,' which includes his memories of the melons from his homeland. Akbar was his grandson.

cau_hoi: What was the name of the uprising in China from 1899 to 1901 against foreigners?
giai_thich: The Boxer Rebellion was a secret society of martial artists (referred to as 'Boxers' by Westerners). They believed they were immune to bullets, attacked foreigners and Christians, and besieged embassies in Beijing. An eight-nation alliance intervened in Beijing to suppress the uprising, and the Qing dynasty had to pay a huge indemnity.

cau_hoi: Which naval battle in 1942 was a turning point in the Pacific, when the U.S. sank four Japanese aircraft carriers?
giai_thich: In June 1942, American experts decrypted Japanese codes and learned of the planned attack on Midway Island. Aircraft from U.S. carriers sank all four participating Japanese carriers. From then on, Japan lost the initiative. This battle demonstrated that aircraft carriers had replaced battleships as the most important weapon at sea.

cau_hoi: What was the capital of the Tang dynasty, one of the largest cities in the world at that time?
giai_thich: Chang'an (now Xi'an) had about 1 million inhabitants in the 8th century, planned in a grid layout with wide boulevards. It was the eastern starting point of the Silk Road, where Persian, Arab merchants, and even Japanese envoys gathered. The capitals of Nara and Kyoto in Japan were modeled after Chang'an.

cau_hoi: Who is the only officially recognized female emperor in Chinese history?
giai_thich: Wu Zetian was originally a consort of Emperor Taizong of Tang and later became the empress of Emperor Gaozong of Tang. In 690, she declared herself emperor, establishing the Zhou dynasty (Wu Zhou), ruling until 705. Empress Dowager Cixi and Empress Lü held significant power but did not officially claim the title of emperor.

cau_hoi: Which empress held real power in the Qing dynasty for nearly 50 years at the end of the 19th century?
giai_thich: Cixi held power from 1861 through three young or weak emperors. She was known for her extravagant spending, reportedly using the navy budget to renovate the Summer Palace, and opposing the reforms of 1898. She died in 1908, just one day after Emperor Guangxu, whom she had previously placed under house arrest.

cau_hoi: The four great inventions of China include paper, the compass, gunpowder, and which other invention?
giai_thich: Woodblock printing technology emerged during the Tang dynasty. The oldest surviving printed book is the Diamond Sutra from 868. During the Song dynasty, Bi Sheng invented movable type printing using clay, about 400 years before Gutenberg. These four inventions had a significant impact on the world: paper and printing spread knowledge, the compass aided navigation, and gunpowder changed warfare.

cau_hoi: Which monk traveled to India during the Tang dynasty to obtain Buddhist scriptures?
giai_thich: In 629, Xuanzang secretly left China, crossing deserts and high mountains to reach India, where he studied at the Buddhist university of Nalanda. In 645, he returned home with over 600 scriptures and spent the rest of his life translating them. His journey inspired the novel 'Journey to the West' featuring the character Tang Seng and Sun Wukong.

cau_hoi: Who founded the Yuan dynasty in China?
giai_thich: Kublai Khan was the grandson of Genghis Khan. In 1271, he established the Great Yuan dynasty and in 1279, he conquered the Southern Song dynasty, becoming the first non-Han ruler to govern all of China. He moved the capital to Dadu (present-day Beijing). Marco Polo served in his court.

cau_hoi: Who founded the Ming dynasty in 1368?
giai_thich: Zhu Yuanzhang came from a poor peasant background, having once been a monk and a beggar. He led the Red Turban army to drive out the Mongols, established the Ming dynasty, and took the reign title Hongwu. He is one of two Chinese emperors of peasant origin, the other being Li Yuan who founded the Tang dynasty.

cau_hoi: Which Ming emperor moved the capital to Beijing and commissioned the construction of the Forbidden City?
giai_thich: Emperor Yongle (Zhu Di), the son of Zhu Yuanzhang, usurped the throne from his nephew and moved the capital from Nanjing to Beijing, his old base. The Forbidden City was constructed from 1406 to 1420. He also sent Zheng He on maritime expeditions and commissioned the Yongle Encyclopedia.

cau_hoi: Which Qing dynasty emperor had the longest reign in Chinese history, lasting 61 years?
giai_thich: Kangxi ascended the throne in 1661 at the age of 7 and ruled until 1722. He quelled the Three Feudatories, reclaimed Taiwan, and signed a border treaty with Russia. His grandson, Qianlong, ruled for 60 years and voluntarily abdicated to avoid surpassing his grandfather's record. The Kangxi Dictionary, compiled during his reign, is still in use.

cau_hoi: Which clan held power over the shogunate during the Edo period in Japan (1603 – 1868)?
giai_thich: In 1603, Tokugawa Ieyasu became Shogun and established the shogunate in Edo (now Tokyo). The Tokugawa clan ruled for about 265 years of peace, with 15 generations of Shoguns. This period saw a flourishing of culture: ukiyo-e woodblock prints, kabuki theater, and Bashō's haiku all thrived.

cau_hoi: The three figures who unified Japan at the end of the 16th century are Oda Nobunaga, Toyotomi Hideyoshi, and who?
giai_thich: The Japanese saying goes: "Nobunaga kneads the dough, Hideyoshi bakes the bread, Ieyasu sits down to eat." Nobunaga initiated the unification, Hideyoshi completed it, while Ieyasu was the last to hold power and established a lasting shogunate. Takeda Shingen and Date Masamune were famous lords but did not unify the country.

cau_hoi: Who won the Battle of Sekigahara in 1600, the decisive battle for power in Japan?
giai_thich: After Hideyoshi's death in 1598, the lords split into two factions. At Sekigahara, Tokugawa Ieyasu's Eastern army defeated the Western army led by Ishida Mitsunari, partly due to some Western lords switching sides during the battle. Three years later, Ieyasu became Shogun. Both Hideyoshi and Nobunaga had died before this battle.

cau_hoi: What is the name of Japan's policy that almost completely restricted foreign relations during the Edo period?
giai_thich: From around 1639, the shogunate prohibited Japanese from traveling abroad and banned most foreigners from entering Japan, fearing the influence of Christianity and European powers. Only the Dutch and Chinese were allowed to trade through Nagasaki port. This policy lasted over 200 years, until Perry's ships arrived.

cau_hoi: During the Sakoku period, where were the Dutch allowed to trade in Nagasaki?
giai_thich: Dejima is a small fan-shaped island of about 1.3 hectares, connected to the mainland by a guarded bridge. The Dutch lived here for over 200 years and were the only channel for Western knowledge to enter Japan. The Japanese referred to this study as "Dutch learning" (rangaku), which included medicine, astronomy, and geography.

cau_hoi: What is the name of the code of honor for samurai, emphasizing loyalty and bravery?
giai_thich: Bushido means "the way of the warrior," emphasizing loyalty to one's lord, courage, maintaining honor, and fearlessness of death. Seppuku is the ritual suicide of a samurai when dishonored. Shinto is Japan's indigenous religion. The book "Bushido: The Soul of Japan" (1900) introduced this concept to the West.

cau_hoi: Which country won the Russo-Japanese War (1904 – 1905)?
giai_thich: Japan defeated Russia at Port Arthur and destroyed the Baltic Fleet in the Battle of Tsushima in 1905, after this fleet had circumnavigated the globe. This was the first time in modern history that an Asian country defeated a European power. This victory inspired anti-colonial movements across Asia, including the Dong Du movement in Vietnam.

cau_hoi: In what year did Japan annex Korea as a colony?
giai_thich: In 1905, Japan made Korea a protectorate, and in 1910 officially annexed it. During 35 years of rule, Japan prohibited the teaching of the Korean language in schools and forced the people to adopt Japanese names. Korea was liberated when Japan surrendered on August 15, 1945, now celebrated as Liberation Day in South Korea.

cau_hoi: What is the name of the last dynasty of Korea, which lasted over 500 years?
giai_thich: The Joseon dynasty was founded by General Yi Seong-gye (Lee Seong-gye) in 1392 and lasted until 1897, when it was renamed the Korean Empire until 1910. Joseon was based on Confucianism and established its capital in Hanyang (now Seoul). Gyeongbokgung Palace and many historical Korean dramas are associated with this dynasty.

cau_hoi: Who founded the empire in Central Asia with the capital Samarkand at the end of the 14th century?
giai_thich: Timur was a Turk-Mongol warrior, injured in the leg, earning the nickname "Timur the Lame" (Tamerlane). He conquered from India to Turkey, notorious for his brutality in war but transformed Samarkand into a magnificent city with turquoise-domed mosques. He is the ancestor of Babur, the founder of the Mughal Empire.

cau_hoi: Which Siamese king modernized the country and abolished slavery in the early 20th century?
giai_thich: King Chulalongkorn reigned for 42 years (1868 – 1910), building railways, establishing post offices, modern schools, and abolishing slavery (completed in 1905). He also ceded some territories to the British and French to maintain Siam's independence. His death date (October 23) is a national holiday in Thailand. His father, King Mongkut, is a character in the film "The King and I."

cau_hoi: What was the old name of Thailand?
giai_thich: In 1939, the government of Prime Minister Phibun changed the country's name from Siam to Thailand (Prathet Thai), meaning "Land of the Free." The name Siam still exists in terms like "Siamese cat" and "Siamese twins" (conjoined twins). Burma is the old name for Myanmar, while Funan and Champa were ancient kingdoms in Cambodia.

cau_hoi: What was the old name of Myanmar?
giai_thich: In 1989, the military government changed the English name of the country from Burma to Myanmar and renamed the capital from Rangoon to Yangon. By 2005, the capital was moved to the new city of Naypyidaw. Some Western countries continued to use the name Burma to protest the military government.

cau_hoi: What was the old name of Sri Lanka?
giai_thich: The island was ruled by the Portuguese, Dutch, and then the British under the name Ceylon, gaining independence in 1948. In 1972, the country changed its name to Sri Lanka, meaning "Resplendent Island." To this day, tea from here is still sold under the famous name "Ceylon tea."

cau_hoi: What name did the Portuguese call Taiwan?
giai_thich: According to legend, when passing by in the mid-16th century, Portuguese sailors exclaimed "Ilha Formosa!", meaning "Beautiful Island!" The name Formosa was used by Westerners for many centuries. From 1895 to 1945, Taiwan was a colony of Japan.

cau_hoi: Who led the independence movement and became the first president of Indonesia?
giai_thich: Sukarno and Mohammad Hatta declared independence on August 17, 1945, right after Japan surrendered. Sukarno became president, while Hatta served as vice president. Sukarno also organized the Asian-African Conference in Bandung in 1955. Suharto was the second president, ruling for over 30 years. Like many Javanese, Sukarno had only one name.

cau_hoi: When did Indonesia declare independence?
giai_thich: On August 17, 1945, Sukarno read the independence proclamation in Jakarta. The Netherlands did not accept it and sent troops back, leading to a four-year war. Under international pressure, the Netherlands recognized Indonesia's independence in December 1949. August 17 is Indonesia's Independence Day.

cau_hoi: When did the U.S. grant independence to the Philippines?
giai_thich: The U.S. took the Philippines from Spain in 1898 and promised independence. In 1935, the Philippines had a self-governing government, but World War II delayed the process. On July 4, 1946, coinciding with U.S. Independence Day, the Philippines became independent. Later, the Philippines moved its Independence Day to June 12, commemorating the declaration of independence from Spain in 1898.

cau_hoi: When did the Federation of Malaya gain independence from Britain?
giai_thich: On August 31, 1957, Prime Minister Tunku Abdul Rahman shouted "Merdeka!" (Independence!) seven times at a stadium in Kuala Lumpur. In 1963, Malaya united with Singapore, Sabah, and Sarawak to form Malaysia. 1965 was the year Singapore separated from Malaysia.

cau_hoi: When did Singapore separate from Malaysia to become an independent nation?
giai_thich: Singapore joined Malaysia in 1963, but political disagreements and ethnic tensions led the Malaysian Parliament to vote for Singapore's separation on August 9, 1965. Prime Minister Lee Kuan Yew cried on television when announcing this news. August 9 is now Singapore's National Day.

cau_hoi: Which Chinese dynasty was the first to issue state-controlled paper money?
giai_thich: In the early 11th century, merchants in Sichuan used promissory notes called "jiaozi" to avoid carrying heavy iron coins. In 1023, the Song Dynasty took over and issued state-backed jiaozi, which was the world's first official paper money. Europe did not have banknotes until the 17th century.

cau_hoi: Which dynasty was the Southern Song finally destroyed by in 1279?
giai_thich: The Song Dynasty resisted the Mongols for about 45 years, longer than most countries attacked by them. In 1279, during the Battle of Yaishan at sea, the official Liu Zhufu carried the young emperor and jumped into the sea to commit suicide. Earlier, in 1127, the Jurchens had occupied the north, forcing the Song to retreat south.

cau_hoi: The An Lushan Rebellion in 755 broke out during the reign of which Tang emperor?
giai_thich: Emperor Xuanzong ushered in a prosperous era but, in his old age, became infatuated with Yang Guifei and delegated power to her relatives. The frontier general An Lushan rebelled and captured Chang'an. The rebellion lasted 8 years, causing a significant population decline, and the Tang Dynasty never regained its former strength.

cau_hoi: What is the real name of Emperor Taizong of Tang, one of China's greatest rulers?
giai_thich: Li Shimin was the second son of Li Yuan, the founder of the Tang Dynasty. He seized the throne through the Xuanwu Gate Incident in 626 but became a wise ruler who listened to advice. His reign is known as the "Zhenguan Era." Li Longji is the real name of Emperor Xuanzong.

cau_hoi: Which Tang poet is known as the "Poet Immortal"?
giai_thich: Li Bai (701 – 762) is famous for his free-spirited, romantic poetry about the moon, wine, and nature, such as the poem "Quiet Night Thoughts," which every Chinese child knows. Because his poetry is like that of an immortal, he is called the "Poet Immortal." His friend Du Fu is known as the "Poet Sage" for his poetry reflecting the suffering of the people.

cau_hoi: In feudal China, what was the examination system for selecting officials based on Confucian classics called?
giai_thich: The imperial examination was established during the Sui Dynasty and flourished during the Tang Dynasty, allowing educated individuals (theoretically including those from poor families) to become officials. Candidates had to memorize the Four Books and Five Classics and write essays according to a set format. The examination system lasted about 1300 years until it was abolished in 1905. Vietnam and Korea also adopted the imperial examination.

cau_hoi: Who is the author of the novel "Journey to the West"?
giai_thich: Ngô Thừa Ân lived during the Ming Dynasty in the 16th century. "Journey to the West" tells the story of Tang Seng along with Sun Wukong, Zhu Bajie, and Sha Wujing on their pilgrimage for scriptures. This is one of the Four Great Classical Novels of Chinese literature, alongside "Romance of the Three Kingdoms" (Luo Guanzhong), "Water Margin" (Wu Cheng'en), and "Dream of the Red Chamber" (Cao Xueqin).

cau_hoi: Who led the Taiping Rebellion (1850 – 1864)?
giai_thich: Hong Xiuquan failed the imperial examinations multiple times. After reading Christian missionary literature, he believed he was the younger brother of Jesus Christ. He established the "Taiping Heavenly Kingdom," occupying half of southern China. This was the bloodiest civil war of the 19th century, potentially causing 20 to 30 million deaths.

cau_hoi: Who became the President of the Republic of China after Sun Yat-sen in 1912 and later proclaimed himself emperor?
giai_thich: Yuan Shikai was a general who commanded the strongest army at the end of the Qing Dynasty. He persuaded Emperor Puyi to abdicate, in exchange for Sun Yat-sen to cede the presidency to him. In 1915, he proclaimed himself emperor, but faced widespread opposition and had to abandon the title after about 83 days, dying in 1916. China then fell into a period of warlord fragmentation.

cau_hoi: When did the Long March of the Chinese Red Army take place?
giai_thich: Surrounded by the Nationalist forces in Jiangxi, the Red Army retreated approximately 10,000 km through snowy mountains and swamps to reach Shaanxi. Of the 86,000 who started, only about 8,000 arrived. During the march, Mao Zedong became the key leader of the Chinese Communist Party.

cau_hoi: In 1937, which city in China did the Japanese army massacre thousands of civilians after capturing it?
giai_thich: In December 1937, the Japanese captured Nanjing, then the capital of the Republic of China, and over about six weeks killed tens of thousands to hundreds of thousands of civilians and prisoners of war. Some foreigners, like German businessman John Rabe, established a "Safety Zone" and saved many lives. This event still affects Sino-Japanese relations today.

cau_hoi: What war did the Marco Polo Bridge Incident in 1937 initiate?
giai_thich: On July 7, 1937, Japanese and Chinese soldiers clashed near the Marco Polo Bridge on the outskirts of Beijing. The incident quickly escalated into a full-scale war that lasted until 1945. This ancient stone bridge features over 400 lion statues, each with a different pose, and was praised by Marco Polo.

cau_hoi: What was the name of the puppet state established by Japan in Northeast China in 1932?
giai_thich: After occupying Manchuria in 1931, Japan established Manchukuo and installed Puyi, the last emperor of the Qing dynasty, as its head, later making him emperor. Real power was held by the Japanese Kwantung Army. The League of Nations did not recognize this state, and Japan withdrew from the League in 1933. Manchukuo collapsed in 1945.

cau_hoi: Who was the first Prime Minister of independent India?
giai_thich: Nehru was a close disciple of Gandhi and served as Prime Minister from 1947 until his death in 1964. He built India into a secular democratic nation, promoting industrial and scientific development. He was also a founding figure of the Non-Aligned Movement. Indian children affectionately called him "Uncle Nehru," and his birthday (November 14) is celebrated as Children's Day in India.

cau_hoi: Who is considered the founder of Pakistan?
giai_thich: Jinnah was a lawyer, leader of the Muslim League, and persistently demanded a separate nation for Muslims. He became the first Governor-General of Pakistan but died just a year later, in 1948. Pakistanis refer to him as "Quaid-e-Azam" (Great Leader). Poet Iqbal was an early proponent of the idea of a separate Islamic state.

cau_hoi: "The Salt March" of 1930 by Gandhi was a protest against what?
giai_thich: British law prohibited Indians from making their own salt and forced them to buy taxed salt. Gandhi and his followers walked about 390 km over 24 days to the coast of Dandi, where he picked up a handful of salt to break the law. Tens of thousands followed suit and were arrested. This simple act drew global attention to India's struggle.

cau_hoi: What is the common name for the 1857 uprising of Indian soldiers against the British East India Company?
giai_thich: Sepoys were Indian soldiers in the army of the British East India Company. Rumors that new cartridges were greased with cow and pig fat (offending both Hindus and Muslims) sparked the uprising. After suppressing the rebellion, the British government dissolved the Company's rule and directly governed India from 1858.

cau_hoi: Which British queen was proclaimed "Empress of India" in 1876?
giai_thich: Prime Minister Disraeli proposed the title "Empress of India" for Victoria in 1876, and the title was ceremoniously proclaimed in Delhi in 1877. In fact, Victoria never visited India, but she learned Hindustani from an Indian servant named Abdul Karim. India was referred to as the "jewel in the crown" of the British Empire.

cau_hoi: Which Mughal emperor is famous for his policy of religious tolerance?
giai_thich: Akbar (reigned 1556 – 1605) was a Muslim but abolished the jizya tax on non-Muslims, married a Hindu woman, and invited scholars of various religions to debate at his "House of Worship." He also appointed Hindus to high positions. Notably, Akbar was likely illiterate but possessed a vast library and listened to others read to him.

cau_hoi: What is the name of the last powerful Hindu empire in South India, with its capital at Hampi?
giai_thich: The Vijayanagara Empire ("City of Victory") existed from 1336 to around 1646. The capital Hampi was one of the largest and richest cities in the world around 1500, according to Portuguese merchants. In 1565, a coalition of Islamic kingdoms defeated the empire and destroyed Hampi. The ruins of Hampi are now a World Heritage site.

cau_hoi: Which empire in India was founded by Shivaji in the 17th century to resist the Mughal dynasty?
giai_thich: Shivaji was a Marathi warrior who used guerrilla tactics in the mountains and built a system of forts in western India. He was crowned king in 1674. The Maratha Empire later became the most powerful force in India during the 18th century until it was defeated by the British. The Indian Navy today honors Shivaji as the founder of the Indian Navy.

cau_hoi: In which region of India was Sikhism founded by Guru Nanak?
giai_thich: Guru Nanak (1469 – 1539) was born in the Punjab region, now divided between India and Pakistan. Sikhism believes in a single God and the equality of all people. The religious center is the Golden Temple in Amritsar, which has a free kitchen serving tens of thousands of people every day. Male Sikh devotees often keep long hair and wear turbans.

cau_hoi: Which Khmer king commissioned the construction of Angkor Wat?
giai_thich: Suryavarman II reigned in the early 12th century and commissioned Angkor Wat as a temple for the god Vishnu, as well as his burial place. The temple was built over approximately 30 years. Unlike most Khmer temples, Angkor Wat faces west, towards the setting sun, associated with death. Jayavarman VII was the later king who built Angkor Thom.

cau_hoi: What is the name of the largest Buddhist temple in the world, located on the island of Java?
giai_thich: Borobudur was built in the 8th – 9th centuries under the Sailendra dynasty, consisting of 9 stacked platforms with about 2,670 reliefs and 504 Buddha statues. Pilgrims walk around from the bottom to the top, symbolizing the path to enlightenment. The temple was covered by volcanic ash and jungle for many centuries and was rediscovered in 1814.

cau_hoi: What is the name of the powerful Hindu-Buddhist kingdom on the island of Java from the 13th to the 16th century?
giai_thich: Majapahit was established in 1293 after the Javanese cleverly exploited and then expelled the Mongol forces. Under Prime Minister Gajah Mada, the influence of Majapahit spread across much of today's Indonesian archipelago. Many Indonesians consider Majapahit to be the precursor of their nation.

cau_hoi: Which maritime kingdom in Sumatra was a center of Buddhism and trade from the 7th to the 13th century?
giai_thich: Srivijaya was centered in Palembang (Sumatra), controlling the Strait of Malacca and taxing merchant ships passing through. In 671, the Chinese monk Yijing stopped here for several months to learn Sanskrit before going to India. He reported that there were over 1,000 monks studying in Srivijaya. The kingdom gradually weakened after the Chola invasion in 1025.

cau_hoi: Which capital of Siam was destroyed by Burmese forces in 1767?
giai_thich: Ayutthaya was the capital of Siam for over 400 years (1351 – 1767) and was once one of the largest cities in the world, with merchants from the Netherlands, Japan, Persia, and China. In 1767, Burmese forces burned the city. Today, the ruins of Ayutthaya, with a Buddha head lying among the roots of a banyan tree, are a World Heritage site.

cau_hoi: Which kingdom is considered the first kingdom of the Thai people, meaning "Land of the Happy Dawn"?
giai_thich: Sukhothai was established around 1238 when the Thai people broke free from Khmer influence. During the reign of King Ramkhamhaeng, the kingdom flourished, and according to tradition, the Thai script was created during this time. Sukhothai was later incorporated into Ayutthaya. The Loy Krathong festival is believed to have originated here.

cau_hoi: After Ayutthaya was destroyed in 1767, where did King Taksin establish a new capital?
giai_thich: Taksin was a Chinese-born general who rallied an army to drive out the Burmese in just a few months. He established the capital in Thonburi, on the west bank of the Chao Phraya River. In 1782, King Rama I moved the capital to the east bank, founding Bangkok. Today, Thonburi is a district of Bangkok.

cau_hoi: What was the capital of the Mongol Empire during Ögedei Khan?
giai_thich: Karakorum is located in the Mongolian steppe and was walled in 1235 during the reign of Ögedei Khan, the son and successor of Genghis Khan. In the palace, there was a giant silver tree that flowed with wine and fermented horse milk, crafted by a French goldsmith. When Kublai Khan moved the capital to Beijing (Khanbaliq), Karakorum declined.

cau_hoi: What was Beijing called during the Yuan dynasty?
giai_thich: Kublai Khan had Dadu built according to a standard grid plan. The Mongols and Turks referred to the city as Khanbaliq, meaning 'City of the Khan.' Marco Polo described it as the most magnificent city in the world. Jinling is the old name for Nanjing, Bianjing was the capital of the Northern Song, and Chang'an was the capital of the Tang dynasty.

cau_hoi: What is the name of the code of laws issued by Genghis Khan for the Mongols?
giai_thich: Yassa is a code of laws that includes regulations on the military, theft, and loyalty. For example, horse theft could be punishable by death, and diplomatic envoys must be protected. Yassa also guaranteed religious freedom within the empire. The original text of the code no longer exists; we only know of it through the writings of historians of that time.

cau_hoi: What was Genghis Khan's real name as a youth?
giai_thich: Temüjin was born around 1162. His father was poisoned by a rival tribe when he was about 9 years old, and his family was abandoned, living in extreme hardship. He gradually gathered allies and united the tribes. In 1206, a council of tribes proclaimed him 'Chinggis Khan' (Genghis Khan), which may mean 'Khan of the four seas' or 'Resilient leader.'

cau_hoi: Which grandson of Genghis Khan captured and destroyed Baghdad in 1258?
giai_thich: Hülegü was the brother of Kublai Khan. In 1258, he captured Baghdad, ending the Abbasid dynasty and destroying the 'House of Wisdom,' a famous library. It is said that the Tigris River turned black from the ink of the books thrown into it. He established the Ilkhanate in Persia.

cau_hoi: In the Battle of Talas in 751, which power did the Tang dynasty fight against?
giai_thich: The Battle of Talas, located in present-day Kazakhstan and Kyrgyzstan, was the only clash between Tang forces and Arab forces. The Tang dynasty lost, and China's influence in Central Asia gradually diminished. According to legend, some Chinese prisoners knew how to make paper, and the craft spread from there to Samarkand and then to the Islamic world and Europe.

cau_hoi: What was the powerful Tibetan kingdom contemporary with the Tang dynasty called?
giai_thich: Tubo was unified by King Songtsen Gampo in the 7th century. He married Princess Wencheng of the Tang dynasty, who is said to have brought Buddhism and Buddha statues to Lhasa. In 763, the Tubo army even captured Chang'an for about two weeks. Nanzhao was a kingdom in Yunnan, while the Turks and Uighurs were nomadic peoples from the north.

cau_hoi: Which ethnic group founded the Qing dynasty?
giai_thich: The Manchus are descendants of the Jurchens, who lived in the Northeast region. The leader Nurhaci unified them in 1616, and in 1636 his son changed the state name to Qing. The Manchus required Han men to shave the front of their heads and braid their hair in the back to show submission. The Mongols established the Yuan dynasty earlier.

cau_hoi: In what year did the Qing army enter Beijing and begin ruling China?
giai_thich: In 1644, the peasant uprising led by Li Zicheng captured Beijing, and the last Ming emperor committed suicide. Ming general Wu Sangui opened the Shanhai Pass for the Qing army to attack Li Zicheng. The Qing army captured Beijing and remained to rule. The year 1368 marks the establishment of the Ming dynasty.

cau_hoi: Which Qing official ordered the destruction of over 1,000 tons of opium in Humen in 1839?
giai_thich: Lin Zexu was sent to Guangzhou to end the opium trade. He confiscated opium from British merchants, mixed it with salt and lime, and dumped it into the sea. He also wrote a letter to Queen Victoria protesting this trade. His actions were used by the British as a pretext to start the Opium War, but he is still regarded as a national hero in China today.

cau_hoi: Which emperor was in power during the "Hundred Days' Reform" of 1898?
giai_thich: Persuaded by scholars Khang Hữu Vi and Lương Khải Siêu, Emperor Quang Tự issued a series of reforms in the Meiji style: new schools, railways, and a modern military. After about 103 days, Empress Dowager Cixi staged a coup, placed Quang Tự under house arrest, and executed six reformers. This failure led many to believe that only a revolution could change China.

cau_hoi: The First Sino-Japanese War (1894 – 1895) broke out due to competition for influence where?
giai_thich: Korea was originally a vassal state of the Qing dynasty, but Japan, after the Meiji Restoration, sought to control the peninsula. When the Donghak Peasant Revolution broke out, both countries sent troops, leading to war. China's modern Beiyang Fleet was defeated. As a result, China had to recognize Korea as "independent" and ceded Taiwan to Japan.

cau_hoi: According to the Treaty of Shimonoseki in 1895, which island did China have to cede to Japan?
giai_thich: The Treaty of Shimonoseki (Mǎ Guān) was signed by Li Hongzhang with Itō Hirobumi. China ceded Taiwan, the Pescadores Islands, and initially the Liaodong Peninsula, while also paying a large indemnity. Russia, Germany, and France later forced Japan to return Liaodong. Taiwan remained a Japanese colony for 50 years, until 1945.

cau_hoi: What did the May Fourth Movement in China in 1919 protest against?
C: The Versailles Conference granting Shandong to Japan
giai_thich: On May 4, 1919, about 3,000 students in Beijing protested upon learning that the Versailles Conference granted German interests in Shandong province to Japan instead of returning them to China. The movement spread into a cultural reform campaign, emphasizing "science and democracy" and using everyday language instead of classical Chinese in writing. May 4th is now celebrated as Youth Day in China.

cau_hoi: Who led the Kuomintang in China after Sun Yat-sen's death?
giai_thich: Chiang Kai-shek was the principal of the Whampoa Military Academy. In 1928, he unified most of China after the Northern Expedition. He led China against Japan during World War II but was defeated by the Communist Party in the civil war, retreating to Taiwan in 1949 and ruling there until his death in 1975.

cau_hoi: Who was the first Premier of the People's Republic of China?
giai_thich: Zhou Enlai served as Premier from 1949 until his death in 1976, while also serving many years as Foreign Minister. He was known as a skilled diplomat, participating in the Geneva Conference in 1954 and the Bandung Conference in 1955. He also hosted U.S. President Nixon in 1972.

cau_hoi: Who initiated China's "reform and opening up" policy starting in 1978?
giai_thich: Deng Xiaoping allowed farmers to cultivate their own land, opened special economic zones like Shenzhen to attract foreign investment. His famous saying was, "It doesn't matter whether a cat is black or white, as long as it catches mice." Thanks to this policy, China became the world's second-largest economy. He was less than 1.6 meters tall.

cau_hoi: Which emperor ruled Japan during World War II?
giai_thich: Hirohito reigned from 1926 to 1989, the longest in Japanese history. On August 15, 1945, for the first time, the Japanese people heard the emperor's voice over the radio as he announced Japan's surrender. After the war, he declared that he was not divine. He was also a marine biologist, having researched and described many marine species.

cau_hoi: Which American general commanded the occupation forces in Japan after 1945?
giai_thich: MacArthur governed Japan from 1945 to 1951. He promoted a new constitution, land reform, granted women the right to vote, and disbanded the Japanese military. He later commanded United Nations forces in the Korean War until he was dismissed by President Truman in 1951 for wanting to expand the war into China.

cau_hoi: What is Article 9 of the 1947 Japanese Constitution famously known for?
B: Granting full powers to the emperor
C: Giving women the right to vote
giai_thich: Article 9 states that the Japanese "forever renounce war" as a right of the nation and will not maintain military forces for warfare. Therefore, Japan's military forces are called the "Self-Defense Forces." This constitution has never been amended even once.

cau_hoi: Which literary work is famous from the Heian period of Japan?
giai_thich: "The Tale of Genji" was written by the noblewoman Murasaki Shikibu in the early 11th century, telling the life and loves of Prince Genji. The work is often referred to as one of the world's first novels. During the Heian period, noblewomen wrote in kana (Japanese script), while men wrote in kanji, so many masterpieces of that time were authored by women.

cau_hoi: Where was the first shogunate of Japan established?
giai_thich: In 1192, Minamoto no Yoritomo was appointed Shogun and established a military government in Kamakura, far from the imperial court in Kyoto. The Kamakura shogunate lasted until 1333 and repelled two Mongol invasions. Today, Kamakura is famous for its outdoor Great Buddha statue, which stands about 11 meters tall.

cau_hoi: What is the current name of the city Edo, where the Tokugawa shogunate was located?
giai_thich: Edo was originally a small fishing village, chosen by Tokugawa Ieyasu as a base in 1590. By the 18th century, Edo had over 1 million inhabitants, likely making it the largest city in the world at that time. In 1868, Emperor Meiji moved here and renamed it Tokyo. Edo Castle is now the residence of the Japanese Imperial Family.

cau_hoi: Who led the invasion of Korea in the years 1592 – 1598?
giai_thich: After unifying Japan, Hideyoshi aimed to conquer the Ming dynasty of China and sent about 150,000 troops through Korea. The Japanese forces faced fierce resistance from the Korean navy, Ming troops, and local militias. When Hideyoshi died in 1598, the Japanese withdrew. The war devastated Korea severely.

cau_hoi: Who is the famous Korean admiral that used the "turtle ship" to defeat the Japanese navy?
giai_thich: Yi Sun-sin won about 23 naval battles without losing any. The turtle ship (geobukseon) had an iron-clad roof, a dragon head that spewed smoke, and many cannons. He died in the Battle of Noryang in 1598 and instructed not to announce his death until the battle was over. A statue of him stands in Gwanghwamun Square, Seoul.

cau_hoi: In 1945, at which line was the Korean Peninsula divided?
giai_thich: In August 1945, two American officers had about 30 minutes to choose a boundary line, and they selected the 38th parallel on a map. The Soviet Union occupied the north, while the United States occupied the south, and in 1948, two separate states were established. The 17th parallel is the dividing line for Vietnam according to the Geneva Agreement of 1954.

cau_hoi: Where was the Korean Armistice Agreement signed in 1953?
giai_thich: Panmunjom is a village located right on the military demarcation line. The agreement was signed on July 27, 1953, after two years of negotiations, establishing the Demilitarized Zone (DMZ) about 4 km wide. Since it was only a ceasefire and not a peace treaty, legally, the two Koreas are still in a state of war. In 2018, leaders from both sides met here.

cau_hoi: Which kingdom first unified most of the Korean Peninsula in the 7th century?
giai_thich: During the Three Kingdoms period, the Korean Peninsula had three kingdoms: Goguryeo, Baekje, and Silla. Silla allied with the Tang dynasty to defeat Baekje (in 660) and Goguryeo (in 668), then expelled Tang forces from the peninsula. The capital of Silla, Gyeongju, is called the "museum without walls" due to its many historical sites.

cau_hoi: The English name "Korea" originates from which dynasty?
giai_thich: The Goryeo dynasty (918 – 1392) traded with Arab merchants, who transmitted this name to the West, eventually becoming "Corea" and then "Korea." The Goryeo period is famous for its celadon pottery and the Tripitaka Koreana, a Buddhist scripture carved on over 81,000 wooden blocks, which still remain intact. Goryeo also printed books using movable metal type earlier than Gutenberg.

cau_hoi: Who established the British trading post in Singapore in 1819?
giai_thich: Thomas Stamford Raffles was an official of the British East India Company. He recognized Singapore's excellent location at the Strait of Malacca and signed an agreement with local leaders to establish a free port. Many landmarks in Singapore bear his name, such as the Raffles Hotel. He also founded the London Zoo.

cau_hoi: Who is the "White Rajah" who ruled the kingdom of Sarawak on the island of Borneo?
giai_thich: In 1841, explorer James Brooke helped the Sultan of Brunei suppress a rebellion and was rewarded with the region of Sarawak, becoming the "Rajah" (king). The Brooke family ruled Sarawak for over 100 years across three generations until 1946. Today, Sarawak is a state of Malaysia.

cau_hoi: Who established the British trading port on the island of Penang in 1786?
giai_thich: Captain Francis Light persuaded the Sultan of Kedah to allow the British to use Penang, promising to help against Siam and Burma. Penang was the first British colony in the Malay Peninsula. Legend has it that he shot silver coins into the jungle to encourage laborers to clear the land. The capital, George Town, is now a World Heritage site.

cau_hoi: In the Battle of Plassey in 1757, who commanded the British East India Company forces to victory?
giai_thich: Robert Clive had about 3,000 troops, but he secretly bribed General Mir Jafar of the Nawab of Bengal's side, so most of the Bengal troops did not engage in battle. This victory allowed the East India Company to control Bengal, the wealthiest region in India, marking the beginning of nearly 200 years of British rule in India. Clive returned to England extremely wealthy.

cau_hoi: Who was the last Viceroy of British India, overseeing the partition in 1947?
giai_thich: Louis Mountbatten, a relative of the British royal family, arrived in India in March 1947. He expedited the independence transfer date to August 1947, nearly a year earlier than planned, causing the partition to occur hastily and chaotically. He later became the first Governor-General of independent India. He was assassinated in 1979.

cau_hoi: In 1919, British troops fired on a crowd of Indians in the city of Amritsar at which garden?
giai_thich: On April 13, 1919, General Reginald Dyer ordered fire on thousands of people gathered in the walled garden, with only a narrow exit. Hundreds died, with official figures around 379, but the actual number could be much higher. This event caused many Indians who were previously loyal to the British to support independence. Poet Tagore returned his knighthood in protest.

cau_hoi: Indian Prime Minister Indira Gandhi was the daughter of whom?
giai_thich: Indira was the only daughter of Nehru. Her "Gandhi" surname comes from her husband, Feroze Gandhi, and is not related to Mahatma Gandhi. She served as Prime Minister twice (1966 – 1977 and 1980 – 1984) and was assassinated by her own bodyguards in 1984. Her son, Rajiv Gandhi, also served as Prime Minister.

cau_hoi: Who chaired the drafting of the Indian Constitution?
giai_thich: Bhimrao Ambedkar came from a class considered "untouchable" (Dalit) and faced discrimination from a young age, but he earned a doctorate in the USA and UK. He led the committee that drafted the Constitution, the longest written constitution in the world, which prohibits caste discrimination. He is a symbol of the struggle for Dalit rights.

cau_hoi: In 1962, which two countries fought in the Himalayas?
giai_thich: The two countries disputed the border in the Aksai Chin region and the eastern mountains. In October 1962, Chinese troops attacked and defeated Indian forces, then unilaterally ceased fire after about a month. The war strained relations between the two countries for a long time, and to this day the border remains undemarcated.

cau_hoi: What is the main disputed territory between India and Pakistan?
giai_thich: In 1947, the Hindu king of Kashmir, where the majority of the population is Muslim, decided to merge with India. The two countries have fought several times over Kashmir (1947, 1965, 1999). Today, the region is divided between India, Pakistan, and a small part controlled by China. Kashmir is also famous for cashmere wool made from mountain goat hair.

cau_hoi: Who was the world's first female prime minister (in 1960) from which country?
giai_thich: Sirimavo Bandaranaike became the Prime Minister of Ceylon (now Sri Lanka) in 1960, after her husband, Prime Minister Solomon Bandaranaike, was assassinated. She served as Prime Minister three times. Her daughter, Chandrika Kumaratunga, later became the President of Sri Lanka. Indira Gandhi (1966) and Golda Meir of Israel (1969) followed her.

cau_hoi: Who was the first female prime minister of a Muslim country?
giai_thich: Benazir Bhutto became the prime minister of Pakistan in 1988 at the age of 35. She was the daughter of former Prime Minister Zulfikar Ali Bhutto and studied at Harvard and Oxford. She served as prime minister twice and was assassinated in 2007 while campaigning. Indira Gandhi was the prime minister of India, a country with a Hindu majority.

cau_hoi: Which Philippine patriot wrote the novel "Noli Me Tangere" and was executed by Spain in 1896?
giai_thich: José Rizal was an ophthalmologist, writer, and spoke over 20 languages. The novel "Noli Me Tangere" (Touch Me Not) exposed the injustices of colonial rule. Despite advocating for peaceful reform, he was executed on December 30, 1896, in Manila. He is a national hero of the Philippines, and December 30 is Rizal Day.

cau_hoi: Who was the president of the First Philippine Republic in 1899?
giai_thich: Emilio Aguinaldo led the revolution against Spain and declared independence on June 12, 1898. In 1899, he established a republic in Malolos, but the U.S. did not recognize it, leading to the Philippine-American War. He was captured in 1901. Aguinaldo lived a long life, passing away in 1964 at the age of 94. Manuel Quezon was the president during the Commonwealth under U.S. rule.

cau_hoi: Which war in 1898 forced Spain to cede the Philippines to the U.S.?
giai_thich: The war began over the issue of Cuba, after the U.S. battleship Maine exploded in Havana harbor. Admiral Dewey's fleet destroyed the Spanish fleet in Manila Bay in just one morning. According to the Treaty of Paris in 1898, the U.S. purchased the Philippines for $20 million and also acquired Guam and Puerto Rico.

cau_hoi: Who was overthrown in the "People Power" revolution in the Philippines in 1986?
giai_thich: Ferdinand Marcos ruled from 1965 and declared martial law in 1972. After the fraudulent election in 1986, about 2 million people gathered on EDSA Avenue in Manila for a peaceful protest, holding flowers and praying in front of tanks. Marcos was forced to flee to Hawaii, and Corazon Aquino became the first female president of the Philippines. His wife, Imelda, is famous for owning over 1,000 pairs of shoes.

cau_hoi: Which leader of Myanmar won the Nobel Peace Prize in 1991?
giai_thich: Aung San Suu Kyi is the daughter of General Aung San, who is considered the father of Myanmar's independence. She led the democracy movement and was under house arrest for a total of about 15 years. She was unable to attend the Nobel Prize ceremony, so her son accepted it on her behalf. Her father, General Aung San, was assassinated in 1947 when she was just 2 years old.

cau_hoi: Which Myanmar national served as Secretary-General of the United Nations?
giai_thich: U Thant served as Secretary-General of the United Nations from 1961 to 1971, being the first Asian to hold this position. He played a crucial role in easing the Cuban Missile Crisis in 1962. Ban Ki-moon (South Korea) is the second Asian, while Kofi Annan is from Ghana.

cau_hoi: When did East Timor officially become an independent nation?
giai_thich: East Timor was once a colony of Portugal, declaring independence in 1975 but was immediately occupied by Indonesia. In the 1999 referendum, about 78% of voters chose independence. After a period of UN administration, East Timor became independent on May 20, 2002, becoming the first new nation of the 21st century.

cau_hoi: What was the name of Jakarta, Indonesia, during Dutch rule?
giai_thich: In 1619, Jan Pieterszoon Coen of the Dutch East India Company captured the city of Jayakarta and rebuilt it as Batavia, named after an ancient tribe in the Netherlands. Batavia became the headquarters of the VOC in Asia, with canals reminiscent of Amsterdam. In 1942, when the Japanese occupied the city, it was renamed Jakarta.

cau_hoi: Which volcano in Indonesia erupted in 1883 with an explosion heard up to 5,000 km away?
giai_thich: The eruption of Krakatoa, located between Java and Sumatra, produced one of the loudest explosions in history, heard as far away as Rodrigues Island in the Indian Ocean. Tsunamis reaching heights of 30-40 meters killed approximately 36,000 people. The ash caused the sky around the world to have a vivid red sunset for many months. Tambora (1815) was an even more powerful eruption.

cau_hoi: The 'Death March' in 1942, when Japanese troops forced American and Filipino prisoners to walk hundreds of kilometers, took place on which peninsula?
giai_thich: In April 1942, after American-Philippine forces surrendered on the Bataan Peninsula, about 70,000 to 80,000 prisoners were forced to march approximately 100 km in the heat, lacking water and being beaten. Thousands died along the way. After the war, the Japanese general responsible was executed. April 9 is celebrated as 'Day of Valor' in the Philippines.

cau_hoi: Which naval battle in 1944 is often regarded as the largest naval battle in history?
giai_thich: In October 1944, when the U.S. landed back in the Philippines, the Japanese navy concentrated almost all its forces to stop them. Over 200,000 sailors and nearly 300 warships participated. The Japanese navy was decimated and never recovered. This was also the first battle where the Japanese used kamikaze pilots in an organized manner.

cau_hoi: The famous photo of American soldiers raising the flag on Mount Suribachi in 1945 was taken on which island?
giai_thich: Iwo Jima is a small volcanic island that the U.S. wanted to capture to use as an airfield. The Japanese dug over 18 km of tunnels and fought almost to the last man. Joe Rosenthal's photo taken on February 23, 1945, won the Pulitzer Prize and became a monument in Washington. The Battle of Okinawa occurred shortly after and was even bloodier.

cau_hoi: The Thai-Burma railway built by prisoners during World War II is associated with which famous bridge over which river?
giai_thich: The Japanese forced about 60,000 Allied prisoners and over 200,000 Asian laborers to build a railway approximately 415 km long through the jungle. Tens of thousands died from disease, starvation, and mistreatment, leading to the railway being called the 'Death Railway.' The film 'The Bridge on the River Kwai' (1957) won 7 Oscars. The bridge is located in Kanchanaburi province, Thailand.

cau_hoi: In what year did the British fortress of Singapore fall to Japanese forces?
giai_thich: The British believed Singapore was an 'impregnable fortress' because it had large guns facing the sea. However, the Japanese attacked from the north, cycling through the Malay Peninsula. On February 15, 1942, about 80,000 British, Indian, and Australian troops surrendered. Churchill called this 'the worst disaster' in British military history.

cau_hoi: The Asian-African Conference in 1955, the precursor to the Non-Aligned Movement, took place in which city?
giai_thich: In April 1955, representatives from 29 Asian and African countries, most of which had just gained independence, met in Bandung (Indonesia). The conference established 10 principles for peaceful coexistence, opposed colonialism, and did not want to align with either the U.S. or the Soviet Union. The Democratic Republic of Vietnam also sent a delegation. The Non-Aligned Movement was officially established in 1961.

cau_hoi: Who led Cambodia to independence from France in 1953?
giai_thich: King Norodom Sihanouk conducted a 'crusade for independence,' campaigning everywhere, and France granted independence to Cambodia on November 9, 1953. He was a unique figure: he was once king, abdicated to enter politics, and then became king again in 1993. He also directed films and composed music.

cau_hoi: Which city was once the capital of the Lan Xang kingdom, now a UNESCO World Heritage site in Laos?
giai_thich: Luang Prabang is located where the Nam Khan River meets the Mekong River and was the capital of Lan Xang until King Setthathirath moved the capital to Vientiane in 1560. The city has over 30 temples and is famous for the sight of monks collecting alms every early morning. The city's name is derived from the Phra Bang Buddha statue.

cau_hoi: The ancient kingdom of Laos, meaning 'Million Elephants,' is which kingdom?
giai_thich: Lan Xang ('Million Elephants under the White Umbrella') was founded by King Fa Ngum in 1353, with the help of the Khmer Empire. The name reflects military strength, as war elephants were the 'tanks' of that time. By the end of the 17th century, Lan Xang split into three kingdoms: Luang Prabang, Vientiane, and Champasak.

cau_hoi: Which kingdom in northern Thailand had its capital at Chiang Mai?
giai_thich: Lan Na ('Million Rice Fields') was established by King Mangrai in the late 13th century, and he built Chiang Mai ('New City') in 1296. Lan Na had its own script and culture and was ruled by Burma for about 200 years before being incorporated into Siam. To this day, people in northern Thailand speak a dialect different from that of Bangkok.

cau_hoi: Which king established the Chakri dynasty, which still reigns in Thailand, in 1782?
giai_thich: General Chao Phraya Chakri ascended the throne in 1782 after King Taksin was deposed, taking the title Rama I and establishing the capital in Bangkok. The full name of Bangkok in Thai is very long, recorded in the record books as one of the longest place names in the world, while Thais often refer to it simply as Krung Thep ("City of Angels"). Since then, Thai kings have all been called Rama, including the current Rama X.

cau_hoi: Which Siamese king regained independence from Myanmar in 1584 and is famous for the elephant-back duel in 1593?
giai_thich: Naresuan lived in Myanmar as a hostage from a young age. In 1584, he declared Ayutthaya independent. In 1593, during the Battle of Nong Sarai, he fought a duel on elephant back and killed the Myanmar prince. The date of this battle is now celebrated as Royal Thai Army Day.

cau_hoi: According to tradition, which Sukhothai king created the Thai script in 1283?
giai_thich: The Ramkhamhaeng stone inscription states that the king created the Thai script in 1283, based on ancient Khmer script. The inscription also describes a prosperous kingdom with the famous phrase "underwater there are fish, in the fields there is rice." Some scholars even debate the true date of the inscription. It is currently displayed at the National Museum in Bangkok.

cau_hoi: Who unified Myanmar and established the Pagan dynasty in the 11th century?
giai_thich: Anawrahta ascended the throne in 1044 and unified the Irrawaddy River basin for the first time. He made Theravada Buddhism the main religion. The Pagan kings built over 10,000 temples and stupas in Bagan, with more than 2,000 structures still remaining today. Pagan declined after Mongol invasions in the late 13th century.

cau_hoi: Which 16th-century Myanmar king established the largest empire in Southeast Asian history?
giai_thich: Bayinnaung (reigned 1550 – 1581) of the Toungoo dynasty conquered Ayutthaya, Lan Na, Lan Xang, and various Shan principalities. Portuguese at that time described his capital Pegu as more magnificent than many European cities. The empire quickly disintegrated after his death. Naresuan of Siam lived at his court as a hostage.

cau_hoi: Who was the last king of Myanmar to be exiled by the British in 1885?
giai_thich: After the Third Anglo-Burmese War (1885), British forces captured the capital Mandalay in just about two weeks. King Thibaw and Queen Supayalat were exiled to Ratnagiri (India), where he died in 1916. Myanmar became a province of British India, only separating in 1937.

cau_hoi: Which Khmer king commissioned the construction of Angkor Thom and the Bayon temple with its massive stone faces?
giai_thich: Jayavarman VII (reigned around 1181 – 1218) was a Khmer king who followed Mahayana Buddhism. He expelled the Champa forces, built Angkor Thom and the Bayon temple featuring over 200 smiling stone faces. He also constructed around 100 hospitals and many rest houses along the roads. The famous Ta Prohm temple, known for its ancient trees growing over the walls, was also built by him.

cau_hoi: Which ancient kingdom in the lower Mekong River, associated with the Óc Eo archaeological site, is considered a precursor to the Khmer states?
giai_thich: Funan developed from around the 1st to the 6th century, serving as a trade center on the maritime route between India and China. At the Óc Eo site (An Giang, Vietnam), archaeologists found Roman coins and Indian jewelry. Funan was later absorbed by Chenla, a vassal state.

cau_hoi: In 1431, which kingdom's forces attacked the Khmer capital Angkor, leading to the relocation of the capital?
giai_thich: The Ayutthaya army besieged and looted Angkor in 1431. After that, the Khmer court gradually moved southward, closer to present-day Phnom Penh, facilitating river trade. Angkor was not completely abandoned: Angkor Wat remains a place of worship for monks. Europeans "rediscovered" Angkor through Henri Mouhot's writings in 1860.

cau_hoi: Who founded the kingdom of Malacca around 1400?
giai_thich: Parameswara was a prince from Palembang (Sumatra). Legend has it that he named Malacca after the melaka tree he was leaning against when he saw a small mouse deer being chased into the river by a hunting dog, which he took as a good omen. He wisely allied with the Ming dynasty for protection against Siam. Hang Tuah is a legendary warrior of Malacca.

cau_hoi: Which Islamic dynasty ruled Northern India before the Mughal Empire was established?
giai_thich: The Delhi Sultanate (1206 – 1526) consisted of five successive dynasties, all of Turkic or Afghan origin. They successfully repelled Mongol invasions into India. The most famous structure from this period is the Qutub Minar, approximately 73 meters tall in Delhi. The last dynasty was the Lodi dynasty, which was defeated by Babur.

cau_hoi: In the First Battle of Panipat in 1526, whom did Babur defeat?
giai_thich: Ibrahim Lodi, the last king of the Delhi Sultanate, had about 100,000 troops and 1,000 war elephants. Babur had only about 12,000 troops but used guns and cannons, causing panic among the elephants. Ibrahim was killed in battle. In 1527, Babur defeated Rana Sanga, the coalition of Rajput kingdoms, at the Battle of Khanwa.

cau_hoi: Which Afghan king temporarily expelled the Mughals and renovated the Grand Trunk Road?
giai_thich: In 1540, Sher Shah Suri defeated Humayun, the son of Babur, forcing him to flee to Persia. During his brief five-year reign, Sher Shah established an efficient administrative system, issued silver rupees, and renovated the Grand Trunk Road connecting Bengal to Afghanistan. After his death, Humayun returned to reclaim the throne.

cau_hoi: Which Persian king plundered Delhi in 1739 and took the famous Peacock Throne?
giai_thich: Nadir Shah defeated the Mughal army at the Battle of Karnal, then plundered Delhi, taking away a vast fortune including the Peacock Throne made of gold and encrusted with jewels, as well as the Koh-i-Noor diamond. This attack significantly weakened the Mughal Empire. The original Peacock Throne was later destroyed and lost.

cau_hoi: Who was the last Mughal emperor, exiled by the British to Rangoon after the uprising of 1857?
giai_thich: Bahadur Shah II, pen name Zafar, was a poet and was over 80 years old when soldiers revolted and proclaimed him leader in 1857. After the British recaptured Delhi, he was tried and exiled to Rangoon (Myanmar), where he died in 1862. The Mughal Empire officially ended after more than 330 years.

cau_hoi: Which Mughal emperor expanded the empire's territory the most by the end of the 17th century?
giai_thich: Aurangzeb ruled for 49 years (1658 – 1707), conquering almost the entire Indian subcontinent. However, he imposed strict Islamic laws, reinstated taxes on non-Muslims, causing discontent among Hindus, Sikhs, and Marathas. Continuous wars drained the treasury, and the empire declined rapidly after his death.

cau_hoi: Which female hero of India fought against the British during the uprising of 1857?
giai_thich: Lakshmibai was the queen of the princely state of Jhansi. When the British sought to annex Jhansi due to the king having no direct heir, she joined the uprising, leading troops and fighting on horseback. In 1858, she sacrificed her life on the battlefield at around 30 years old. Even the opposing British general called her "the most dangerous of the rebel leaders."

cau_hoi: Who is the only woman to have ruled the Delhi Sultanate?
giai_thich: Razia ascended the throne in 1236, chosen by her father, King Iltutmish, instead of his sons. She dressed as a man, rode elephants into battle, and personally handled state affairs, which caused opposition from the nobles. She was overthrown and killed in 1240. Nur Jahan was a powerful Mughal empress but did not rule.

cau_hoi: Which political party led the Indian independence movement and was founded in 1885?
giai_thich: The Indian National Congress was founded in 1885 in Bombay, initially seeking greater participation in governance. Under Gandhi's leadership from the 1920s, the party became a mass movement demanding independence. After 1947, the party led India for most of the time with prime ministers like Nehru and Indira Gandhi.

cau_hoi: In which year did Rabindranath Tagore, the first Asian Nobel laureate, receive the Nobel Prize in Literature?
giai_thich: Tagore was a Bengali poet, writer, musician, and painter. He received the Nobel Prize for his poetry collection "Gitanjali" (Song Offerings). Notably, he is the author of the national anthems of two countries: India ("Jana Gana Mana") and Bangladesh ("Amar Shonar Bangla"). The national anthem of Sri Lanka is also influenced by him.

cau_hoi: When did China's "one child policy" begin to be implemented?
giai_thich: The policy was implemented around 1979 – 1980 to curb the population growth rate when China had nearly 1 billion people. There were many exceptions in rural areas and among ethnic minorities. The policy caused gender imbalance and rapid aging of the population. In 2016, China allowed two children, and in 2021, three children.

cau_hoi: When did the "Great Leap Forward" campaign in China begin?
giai_thich: In 1958, Mao Zedong launched the Great Leap Forward to quickly catch up with Britain in steel production. Farmers were organized into communes and had to smelt steel in backyard furnaces, neglecting their fields. Combined with exaggerated production reports, the campaign led to a great famine (1959 – 1961), causing tens of millions of deaths.

cau_hoi: When did the Cultural Revolution in China begin?
giai_thich: In 1966, Mao Zedong launched the Cultural Revolution to eliminate those considered to be following the "capitalist path" and to consolidate power. Red Guard groups, consisting of students, denounced teachers and officials, destroying many temples and historical sites. Universities were closed for many years. The movement ended with Mao's death in 1976.

cau_hoi: Which city hosted the first Summer Olympics in Asia in 1964?
giai_thich: The Tokyo 1964 Olympics marked Japan's resurgence just about 19 years after its defeat in World War II. The Olympic torchbearer was Yoshinori Sakai, born on August 6, 1945, in Hiroshima, the exact day the city was bombed. Judo was included in the Olympics for the first time. Sapporo hosted the Winter Olympics in 1972.

cau_hoi: Which city was connected by the first Shinkansen high-speed train line inaugurated in 1964?
giai_thich: The Tōkaidō Shinkansen line was inaugurated on October 1, 1964, just before the Tokyo Olympics, and was the world's first high-speed rail line. The train runs at about 210 km/h, reducing the travel time from Tokyo to Osaka from nearly 7 hours to about 4 hours. Due to its rounded nose, it is called the "bullet train." The Shinkansen is famous for its punctuality.

cau_hoi: In which year did Seoul host the Summer Olympics?
giai_thich: The Seoul 1988 Olympics was the first Olympic Games in 12 years to include both the United States and the Soviet bloc after the boycotts of 1980 and 1984. The event showcased South Korea as a rapidly developing industrial nation. The year 2002 was when South Korea and Japan co-hosted the FIFA World Cup.

cau_hoi: Which country's model was the Meiji Constitution of Japan in 1889 based on?
giai_thich: Itō Hirobumi traveled to Europe to study various countries and chose the Prussian model, where the emperor retained significant power, rather than the British or American models. The Meiji Constitution was the first modern constitution in Asia, establishing a parliament but granting supreme power to the emperor. This constitution remained in effect until 1947.
