cau_hoi: Who led the last major samurai uprising in 1877?
giai_thich: Saigō Takamori was instrumental in restoring Emperor Meiji to power but later became disillusioned as the samurai lost all privileges. He led about 40,000 samurai from Satsuma in rebellion but was defeated by the new-style army (composed of armed farmers). He is regarded as the "last samurai," and a statue of him with a dog stands in Ueno Park, Tokyo.

cau_hoi: Who was the first Prime Minister of Japan?
giai_thich: Itō Hirobumi became Prime Minister in 1885 when the cabinet system was established and held the position four times. He was the principal author of the Meiji Constitution. In his youth, he secretly went to England to study, despite Japanese laws at the time prohibiting travel abroad. His portrait was once printed on the 1,000 yen note.

cau_hoi: In 1909, which Korean patriot assassinated Itō Hirobumi at Harbin station?
giai_thich: Itō was the first Governor-General of Japan in Korea, who forced Korea to become a protectorate. On October 26, 1909, An Jung-geun shot him at Harbin station (Manchuria). An was executed in 1910. In Korea, An Jung-geun is honored as a national hero, while in Japan, Itō is regarded as a modern nation-builder.

cau_hoi: Who was the first president of South Korea?
giai_thich: Syngman Rhee operated independently in the U.S. for many years and held a Ph.D. from Princeton University. He served as president from 1948, when the Republic of Korea was established, until 1960. The fraudulent election of 1960 led to a student protest movement (April 19 Revolution), forcing him to resign and live in exile in Hawaii.

cau_hoi: What was the name of the nationwide independence movement in Korea against Japan that took place on March 1, 1919?
giai_thich: On March 1, 1919, 33 leaders signed the Declaration of Independence in Seoul, and millions of people across the peninsula took to the streets shouting "Long live independence!" The Japanese military suppressed the movement violently, resulting in thousands of deaths. 17-year-old student Yu Gwan-sun died in prison and became a symbol of the movement. March 1 is a national holiday in South Korea.

cau_hoi: Which peasant uprising in Korea in 1894 led to which war?
giai_thich: Eastern Learning ("Eastern Doctrine") was a new religion against corruption and foreign influence. When the peasants revolted in 1894, the Joseon court requested troops from the Qing dynasty, and Japan also sent troops. After suppressing the uprising, Japanese and Qing forces clashed, leading to the First Sino-Japanese War.

cau_hoi: Which Korean queen was assassinated by a Japanese assassin in the palace in 1895?
giai_thich: Queen Myeongseong was a significant influence in the court, seeking to rely on Russia to counter Japanese influence. In the early hours of October 8, 1895, a group of Japanese infiltrated Gyeongbokgung Palace and killed her. This event caused King Gojong to take refuge in the Russian embassy for about a year. Two years later, she was posthumously honored as queen.

cau_hoi: Who was the first queen of Korea, known for building the Cheomseongdae observatory?
giai_thich: Seondeok reigned over the Silla kingdom from 632 to 647. The Cheomseongdae observatory in Gyeongju, approximately 9 meters tall, is considered the oldest surviving astronomical observatory in East Asia. It was built with around 362 stone blocks, which some believe correspond to the number of days in the lunar year. She was the first of three queens of Silla.

cau_hoi: In the Battle of Myeongnyang in 1597, how many warships did Admiral Yi Sun-sin have to fight against the Japanese fleet?
giai_thich: After the Korean navy was defeated when he was dismissed, Yi Sun-sin had only 13 warships left. He lured about 130 Japanese ships into the narrow Myeongnyang Strait, where the current changed direction, and sank or damaged about 30 enemy ships without losing any of his own. His famous pre-battle saying was "I still have 12 ships left" (the 13th was added later).

cau_hoi: In 1582, where was Oda Nobunaga betrayed and committed suicide?
giai_thich: When Nobunaga stayed at Honnō-ji Temple with very few guards, his general Akechi Mitsuhide unexpectedly surrounded the temple. Nobunaga committed suicide as the temple burned, and his body was never found. Just 13 days later, Toyotomi Hideyoshi defeated Mitsuhide to avenge his lord.

cau_hoi: Who betrayed and attacked Oda Nobunaga in 1582?
giai_thich: Akechi Mitsuhide was one of Nobunaga's best generals. Historians still debate why he betrayed him: possibly due to humiliation, ambition, or political reasons. He held power for only about 13 days before being defeated by Hideyoshi, leading the Japanese to refer to a brief power as "the realm for three days."

cau_hoi: In which city is the Great Buddha statue made of bronze located in Tōdai-ji, one of the largest bronze Buddha statues in the world?
giai_thich: The Great Buddha statue is approximately 15 meters tall, commissioned by Emperor Shōmu and completed in 752, using nearly all the bronze available in Japan at that time. The main hall housing the statue was once the largest wooden structure in the world. Nara is also home to over 1,000 deer that roam freely, considered messengers of the gods.

cau_hoi: Which regent prince issued the "Seventeen Article Constitution" in 604 and promoted Buddhism in Japan?
giai_thich: Prince Shōtoku served as regent for Empress Suiko. His Seventeen Article Constitution was essentially moral teachings for officials, beginning with the phrase "Harmony is to be valued." He commissioned the construction of Hōryū-ji Temple, which contains some of the oldest wooden structures in the world. Legend has it that he could hear ten people speaking at once.

cau_hoi: What is the name of the oldest surviving historical text of Japan, completed in 712?
giai_thich: Kojiki records the myths about the formation of Japan, such as the Sun Goddess Amaterasu and the lineage of the Emperors. The book was transcribed from the recitations of Hieda no Are. Nihon Shoki was published in 720, eight years later. Manyōshū is the oldest anthology of poetry in Japan.

cau_hoi: In what year did Emperor Kammu move the capital to Heian-kyō (Kyoto)?
giai_thich: Emperor Kammu moved from Nara partly to avoid the excessive influence of Buddhist temples in politics. Heian-kyō ("Capital of Peace") was planned in a grid layout similar to Chang'an. The Heian period (794 – 1185) was the golden age of Japanese court culture. The year 710 was when Nara became the capital.

cau_hoi: Who established the Kamakura Shogunate, the first military government of Japan?
giai_thich: Minamoto no Yoritomo led the Minamoto clan to victory over the Taira clan, and in 1192 he was appointed Shogun. He established the government in Kamakura, far from the Kyoto court. After his death, the Hōjō clan, his wife's family, held real power. Hōjō Tokimune was the commander against the Mongol forces.

cau_hoi: The Battle of Dan-no-ura in 1185 ended the Genpei War. Which clan was defeated in this battle?
giai_thich: In the naval battle at the strait of Dan-no-ura, the Taira clan was completely defeated. Many Taira members jumped into the sea, including the 6-year-old Emperor Antoku, who was carried by his grandmother. Legend has it that the souls of the Taira warriors transformed into Heike crabs, whose shells resemble the angry faces of samurai.

cau_hoi: Who established the second Shogunate of Japan, the Muromachi Shogunate (Ashikaga)?
giai_thich: Ashikaga Takauji initially helped Emperor Go-Daigo overthrow the Kamakura Shogunate in 1333 but later turned against him. In 1338, Takauji became Shogun, establishing the Shogunate in the Muromachi district of Kyoto. During this period, tea ceremony art, Noh theater, and Zen gardens flourished, but central authority weakened.

cau_hoi: Which Shogun commissioned the construction of Kinkaku-ji (Golden Pavilion) in Kyoto?
giai_thich: Ashikaga Yoshimitsu built Kinkaku-ji as a retirement villa in 1397, with the upper two floors covered in gold leaf. After his death, it became a Zen temple. In 1950, a young monk set fire to the temple, and the current building was reconstructed in 1955. This story inspired a novel by author Mishima Yukio.

cau_hoi: Who was the last Shogun of Japan?
giai_thich: Tokugawa Yoshinobu became Shogun in 1867 and just a few months later returned power to the Emperor. After the defeat in the Boshin War, he lived in seclusion in Shizuoka, pursuing hobbies like photography and cycling, and lived until 1913. Tokugawa Ieyasu was the first Shogun of this clan.

cau_hoi: The Treaty of Kanagawa in 1854, which ended Japan's isolation policy, was signed with which country?
giai_thich: When Admiral Perry returned in 1854 with 9 warships, the Shogunate signed the Treaty of Kanagawa, opening the ports of Shimoda and Hakodate to American supply ships and allowing the U.S. to establish a consulate. Soon after, Britain, Russia, and the Netherlands also demanded similar treaties. The Shogunate's weakness against foreigners caused discontent among many samurai.

cau_hoi: The Boshin War (1868 – 1869) in Japan was a conflict between which two forces?
B: The Emperor's forces and the Tokugawa Shogunate
giai_thich: The Satsuma and Chōshū domains supported the Emperor, fighting against those loyal to the Shogunate. The Imperial forces won thanks to modern weapons purchased from the West. The final battle took place in Hakodate (Hokkaido), where Shogunate supporters had briefly established the "Ezo Republic." This victory paved the way for the Meiji Restoration.

cau_hoi: Before being annexed by Japan in 1879, the Okinawa Islands were an independent kingdom known as what?
giai_thich: The Ryukyu Kingdom prospered by acting as an intermediary for trade between China, Japan, and Southeast Asia, and paying tribute to both the Ming and Qing dynasties as well as the Satsuma domain of Japan. In 1879, Japan annexed the kingdom into Okinawa Prefecture. Shuri Castle, the palace of the Ryukyu kings, burned down in 2019 and is currently being rebuilt.

cau_hoi: Which indigenous people live on the island of Hokkaido (formerly known as Ezo)?
giai_thich: The Ainu people have their own language, beliefs, and clothing, living by hunting, fishing, and bear worship. During the Meiji era, the Japanese government seized their land and banned many traditional customs. It wasn't until 2019 that Japan officially recognized the Ainu as an indigenous people. Jōmon is the name of a prehistoric period in Japan.

cau_hoi: The Kuril Islands (referred to by the Japanese as the Northern Territories) are currently disputed between Japan and which country?
giai_thich: At the end of World War II, the Soviet Union occupied the entire Kuril Islands and expelled about 17,000 Japanese residents. Japan claims the four southernmost islands. Due to this dispute, Japan and Russia have yet to sign a formal peace treaty to conclude World War II. With South Korea, Japan disputes another island group, Dokdo/Takeshima.

cau_hoi: Which Confucian scholar from Korea is depicted on the 1,000 won banknote of South Korea?
giai_thich: Yi Hwang (1501 – 1570), known as Toegye, was a leading Neo-Confucian scholar during the Joseon period and founded the Dosan Seowon library. Other South Korean banknotes also feature notable figures: 5,000 won is Yulgok, 10,000 won is King Sejong, and 50,000 won is Shin Saimdang, Yulgok's mother. The mother and son Yulgok are the only case of two individuals appearing on banknotes.

cau_hoi: During the Joseon period, what was the class of scholar-nobles holding official positions in the court called?
giai_thich: Yangban means "two classes," referring to the civil and military classes in the court. They studied Confucianism, took civil service exams to become officials, and enjoyed many privileges. According to the beliefs of that time, yangban were not allowed to do manual labor or engage in trade. Brahmin is the highest priestly caste in India, while samurai and daimyo belong to Japanese society.

cau_hoi: The Treaty of Nerchinsk in 1689, the first treaty between China and a European power, was signed by the Qing dynasty with which country?
giai_thich: After clashes along the Amur River, the Qing dynasty under Kangxi and Russia signed a treaty to delineate borders. The document was written in Latin, Russian, Manchu, and Chinese. Jesuit missionaries serving in the Qing court acted as translators, as Latin was a common language understood by both sides.

cau_hoi: In 1793, British envoy Macartney visited China to request an expansion of trade and met which emperor?
giai_thich: Macartney brought many gifts such as clocks and telescopes but refused to kneel according to protocol. Qianlong sent a letter to King George III, stating that China "lacked nothing" and did not need foreign goods. This failure contributed to Britain using force to open China nearly 50 years later.

cau_hoi: According to the Treaty of Beijing in 1860, Russia gained coastal land where which port city was established in the same year?
giai_thich: Taking advantage of the Qing dynasty's defeat by Britain and France, Russia acted as a mediator and was ceded land east of the Ussuri River. Russia established the port of Vladivostok, meaning "Ruling the East," on this new territory. Vladivostok became the base of the Russian Pacific Fleet and the terminus of the Trans-Siberian Railway.

cau_hoi: The Summer Palace, the magnificent palace of the Qing emperors, was burned by British and French troops in which year?
giai_thich: During the Second Opium War, after a group of British and French envoys was captured and killed, Lord Elgin ordered the burning of the Summer Palace as retaliation. The fire lasted for several days, destroying hundreds of buildings, and countless treasures were looted and taken back to Europe. Writer Victor Hugo called this act the work of "two thieves."

cau_hoi: Where did the Taiping Heavenly Kingdom establish its capital and call it "Tianjing"?
giai_thich: In 1853, Taiping forces captured Nanjing and renamed it Tianjing ("Heavenly Capital"). They banned opium, prohibited foot-binding for women, and advocated for land redistribution. However, internal leadership divisions led to mutual massacres. In 1864, Qing forces recaptured Nanjing, and Hong Xiuquan had died a few weeks earlier.

cau_hoi: Which Qing minister established the "Xiang Army" in Hunan to suppress the Taiping Heavenly Kingdom?
giai_thich: Zeng Guofan was a Confucian scholar, not a military official, but he organized a loyal and disciplined local army in his home province of Hunan. This army was the main force that defeated the Taiping Heavenly Kingdom. He also initiated the Westernization Movement, learning Western military techniques. His student, Li Hongzhang, established the Huai Army.

cau_hoi: What is the name of the document from 1901 that ended the Boxer Rebellion, forcing the Qing dynasty to pay a huge indemnity?
giai_thich: In 1901, the year of the Metal Ox, according to the protocol, the Qing dynasty had to pay 450 million taels of silver, equivalent to about one tael for each Chinese citizen at that time, to be paid over 39 years. Foreign troops were also allowed to be stationed in Beijing to protect their embassies. Later, the United States used part of the indemnity to establish Tsinghua University.

cau_hoi: Which uprising on October 10, 1911, marked the beginning of the Xinhai Revolution?
giai_thich: An accidental bomb explosion in the secret base of the revolutionary group in Hankou revealed the list of members. With no way to retreat, newly recruited soldiers in Wuchang revolted and seized the city. Within weeks, many provinces declared independence from the Qing dynasty. October 10 ("Double Ten") is Taiwan's National Day.

cau_hoi: Which conference in 1935 during the Long March solidified Mao Zedong's leadership role?
giai_thich: In January 1935, after heavy losses, the leadership of the Chinese Communist Party met in Zunyi (Guizhou). The conference criticized the old military tactics proposed by Soviet advisor Otto Braun and brought Mao into the military leadership. This is considered the turning point that elevated Mao to a key leadership position.

cau_hoi: After the Long March, where did the Chinese Communist Party establish its main base until 1947?
giai_thich: Yan'an is located in Shaanxi Province, in a region of golden earth. Here, the Party leaders lived and worked in caves dug into the hillsides. From Yan'an, the Party built its forces and fought against the Japanese. American journalist Edgar Snow visited here in 1936 and wrote the book "Red Star Over China," introducing Mao to the world.

cau_hoi: Which city served as the wartime capital of the Nationalist government from 1938 to 1945?
giai_thich: After Nanjing and Wuhan fell, Chiang Kai-shek's government retreated to Chongqing, a mountainous city in Sichuan protected by mountain ranges and the Yangtze River gorge. The Japanese air force bombed Chongqing hundreds of times, and the people had to take shelter in caves dug into the rock. In 1945, Mao came here to negotiate with Chiang but was unsuccessful.

cau_hoi: During the Xi'an Incident in 1936, which figure was General Zhang Xueliang holding captive?
giai_thich: Zhang Xueliang, whose homeland Manchuria was occupied by Japan, wanted Chiang to stop fighting the Communist Party to unite against the Japanese. He captured Chiang in Xi'an and forced him to agree to establish the Second United Front. Afterward, Chiang kept Zhang under house arrest for over 50 years. Zhang lived to be 100 years old and died in Hawaii in 2001.

cau_hoi: The Mukden Incident in 1931 was used by Japan as a pretext to invade which region?
giai_thich: On September 18, 1931, a Japanese officer blew up a section of railway managed by Japan near Mukden (now Shenyang) and blamed China. The Kwantung Army used this as an excuse to occupy all of Manchuria within months, without needing permission from the Tokyo government. The explosion was so minor that a train was able to pass through immediately afterward.

cau_hoi: In what year did the People's Republic of China replace the Republic of China (Taiwan) in holding China's seat at the United Nations?
giai_thich: On October 25, 1971, the United Nations General Assembly adopted Resolution 2758, granting China's seat, including the permanent seat on the Security Council, to Beijing. The Taiwanese delegation left the United Nations. 1979 was the year the United States officially established diplomatic relations with Beijing.

cau_hoi: Which U.S. president made a historic visit to China in 1972?
giai_thich: In February 1972, Nixon visited China for a week, meeting Mao Zedong and Zhou Enlai, ending over 20 years of no relations between the two countries. The two sides signed the Shanghai Communiqué. Nixon called it "the week that changed the world." Advisor Henry Kissinger had secretly visited Beijing since 1971 to prepare.

cau_hoi: In what year did the "ping-pong diplomacy" event occur, when the U.S. table tennis team was invited to visit China?
giai_thich: At the World Championships in Japan in 1971, American player Glenn Cowan accidentally boarded the Chinese team's bus. Chinese player Zhuang Zedong gifted him a silk painting. Just a few days later, China invited the U.S. team to visit, paving the way for Nixon's trip. This is a famous example of how sports helped mend international relations.

cau_hoi: Which leader is known as "Bangabandhu" (Friend of Bengal), the father of Bangladesh?
giai_thich: Sheikh Mujibur Rahman led the Awami League to a significant victory in the 1970 elections, but the West Pakistani government did not transfer power to him. He was arrested when Bangladesh declared independence in 1971 and was released after the victory. In 1975, he was assassinated along with many family members. His daughter, Sheikh Hasina, later became the Prime Minister.

cau_hoi: Which British lawyer drew the border dividing India and Pakistan in 1947?
giai_thich: Cyril Radcliffe had never been to India before and had only about 5 weeks to draw the border through Punjab and Bengal, using outdated maps and population data. The border was announced on August 17, 1947, two days after independence. Radcliffe returned home, burned all documents, and refused to accept payment.

cau_hoi: Which Viceroy divided Bengal in two in 1905, causing a major wave of protests?
giai_thich: Lord Curzon claimed that the division of Bengal was for easier administration, but many Indians believed this was a "divide and rule" policy, separating Hindus and Muslims. Bengalis protested by boycotting British goods and only using local products (the Swadeshi movement). In 1911, the British had to reverse the division and move the capital from Calcutta to Delhi.

cau_hoi: "Doctrine of Lapse," which allowed the British to annex Indian princely states without direct heirs, is associated with which Viceroy?
giai_thich: Lord Dalhousie (Viceroy 1848 – 1856) used this doctrine to annex many princely states like Satara, Jhansi, and Nagpur, as the rulers there only had adopted heirs. He also built the first railways and telegraph lines in India. Discontent with this doctrine was one of the causes of the uprising in 1857.

cau_hoi: After the Battle of Buxar in 1764, which Mughal emperor granted the British East India Company the right to collect taxes (diwani) in which region?
giai_thich: In 1765, Robert Clive received the diwani rights for Bengal, Bihar, and Orissa from Mughal Emperor Shah Alam II. From a trading company, the East India Company became the tax authority for tens of millions of people. Just a few years later, the Bengal famine of 1770 killed about one-third of the region's population.

cau_hoi: Which Sikh king unified Punjab and was known as the "Lion of Punjab"?
giai_thich: Ranjit Singh established the Sikh Empire in 1799 with its capital in Lahore and was the last ruler in India to maintain independence from the British while alive. He was blind in one eye due to smallpox as a child. He gilded the Harmandir Sahib in Amritsar, which is now known as the Golden Temple. After his death in 1839, the British annexed Punjab in 1849.

cau_hoi: Which famous diamond originated in India and is now set in a crown of the British Royal Family?
giai_thich: Koh-i-Noor ("Mountain of Light") has passed through the hands of Mughal emperors, Nadir Shah, Afghan kings, and Ranjit Singh. In 1849, the British took the diamond from the young Sikh king Duleep Singh and presented it to Queen Victoria. India, Pakistan, and Afghanistan have all claimed it back. The Cullinan diamond belongs to the British Royal Family but originated from South Africa.

cau_hoi: According to the Anglo-Dutch Treaty of 1824, the Malay Peninsula was under British influence, while which region was under Dutch control?
giai_thich: The two countries exchanged territories: the British ceded Bencoolen (Sumatra) to the Dutch, while the Dutch ceded Malacca to the British. The boundary was drawn through the Strait of Malacca. This boundary later nearly became the border between Malaysia and Indonesia. Therefore, the Malays on both sides of the strait share a common culture but belong to different countries.

cau_hoi: Who was the Javanese prince that led the Java War (1825 – 1830) against the Dutch?
giai_thich: Diponegoro revolted when the Dutch built a road cutting through his ancestral grave site. The war lasted 5 years, resulting in about 200,000 Javanese deaths. In 1830, he was lured into negotiations by the Dutch, then captured and exiled to Sulawesi. Today he is regarded as a national hero of Indonesia, with many streets and universities named after him.

cau_hoi: Which female hero of Indonesia was a pioneer in advocating for women's right to education?
giai_thich: Kartini (1879 – 1904) was the daughter of a Javanese official. She wrote many letters in Dutch to friends, opposing the prohibition of girls from attending school and the practice of forced marriages. After her death at the age of 25, her letters were published as a book titled "From Darkness to Light." Her birthday (April 21) is celebrated as Kartini Day in Indonesia.

cau_hoi: In 1025, which empire from South India attacked the Srivijaya kingdom by sea?
giai_thich: King Rajendra I of the Chola dynasty had a powerful navy that crossed the Bay of Bengal to attack several ports of Srivijaya in Sumatra and the Malay Peninsula. This was one of the few maritime expeditions by an Indian kingdom. The Chola are also famous for their exquisitely crafted bronze statues of the dancing god Shiva.

cau_hoi: The Prambanan temple complex on the island of Java is dedicated to the gods of which religion?
giai_thich: Prambanan was built in the 9th century and is the largest Hindu temple complex in Indonesia, dedicated to the three main gods Brahma, Vishnu, and Shiva. The main tower is about 47 meters tall. The temple is located only about 18 km from Borobudur, the Buddhist temple, indicating that both religions coexisted in Java at that time. Today, the majority of Indonesians are Muslim.

cau_hoi: Which Ming emperor mysteriously disappeared when Zhu Di usurped the throne in 1402?
giai_thich: Jianwen was the grandson and successor of Zhu Yuanzhang. He aimed to reduce the power of his uncles who were granted princely titles, prompting his uncle, the Prince of Yan Zhu Di, to rebel. When Zhu Di's forces entered Nanjing, the palace caught fire, and Jianwen vanished. Legend has it that he disguised himself as a monk to escape, and some theories suggest that Zheng He’s voyages were partly to search for him.

cau_hoi: In the Tumu Crisis of 1449, which Ming emperor was captured by the Oirat (Wokou) forces?
giai_thich: Emperor Zhengtong, following the advice of the eunuch Wang Zhen, personally led troops against the Oirat at the northern border and was defeated at Tumu Fortress. He was taken prisoner, and his younger brother ascended the throne in his place. A year later, he was released and staged a coup to reclaim the throne under the new reign title of Tianshun.

cau_hoi: Which Italian Jesuit missionary arrived in Beijing in 1601 and collaborated with Xu Guangqi to translate Euclid's geometry into Chinese?
giai_thich: Matteo Ricci learned Chinese, dressed as a Confucian scholar, and introduced European science to the Ming court, including clocks, world maps, and mathematics. The world map he created in 1602 was the first to show the Americas to the Chinese. He was the first Westerner to be buried in Beijing. Alexandre de Rhodes was a missionary in Vietnam.

cau_hoi: In which year did Saint Francis Xavier, the first Christian missionary to Japan, arrive?
giai_thich: Francis Xavier was one of the founders of the Jesuit order, arriving in Kagoshima in 1549. He preached for about two years and noted that the Japanese highly respected Chinese culture, prompting him to wish to evangelize in China. He died in 1552 on an island near Guangzhou while waiting to enter the mainland. By the end of the 16th century, Japan had about 300,000 Christian converts.

cau_hoi: What was the consequence of the Shimabara Rebellion (1637 – 1638) by farmers, most of whom were Christians?
D: Completion of the shogunate's isolation policy
giai_thich: Burdened by heavy taxes and religious persecution, about 30,000 farmers and disaffected samurai in the Shimabara Peninsula revolted, led by the 16-year-old Amakusa Shirō. The shogunate suppressed the uprising brutally. Subsequently, the shogunate expelled the Portuguese in 1639 and completed its isolation policy (sakoku), allowing only the Dutch to remain in Dejima.

cau_hoi: Which peasant leader captured Beijing in 1644, causing Emperor Chongzhen, the last Ming ruler, to commit suicide?
giai_thich: Li Zicheng was originally a courier in the postal system who lost his job when the court cut spending. He formed a peasant army with the slogan of no taxes. When his forces entered Beijing, Emperor Chongzhen hanged himself on Coal Hill after the Forbidden City. Li Zicheng held Beijing for only about 40 days before being driven out by the Qing forces.

cau_hoi: Which Ming general opened the Shanhai Pass for the Qing army to enter China in 1644?
giai_thich: Wu Sangui was stationed at Shanhai Pass, the gateway where the Great Wall meets the sea. When Li Zicheng captured Beijing and took his family hostage, Wu allied with the Qing forces to fight Li. Later, he was granted a princely title in Yunnan, but he eventually rebelled against the Qing during the Three Feudatories Rebellion and died in 1678.

cau_hoi: In 1662, Zheng Chenggong (Koxinga) expelled the Dutch from which island?
giai_thich: Zheng Chenggong was the son of a Chinese merchant-pirate and a Japanese woman. He remained loyal to the Ming dynasty and continued to resist the Qing. In 1662, after a 9-month siege, he forced the Dutch to surrender at Fort Zeelandia and established a government in Taiwan. He died just a few months later at the age of 37. In 1683, the Qing conquered Taiwan.

cau_hoi: The Three Feudal Lords Rebellion (1673 – 1681) was suppressed during the reign of which Qing emperor?
giai_thich: Three Han generals who assisted the Qing, including Wu Sangui, were granted titles in the south and held significant power. When Emperor Kangxi, at about 19 years old, decided to abolish the feudal lords, they revolted. After 8 years of war, Kangxi emerged victorious and consolidated Qing power across China.

cau_hoi: Which massive collection of books was compiled during the reign of Emperor Qianlong?
giai_thich: The Complete Library in Four Sections was compiled from 1773 to around 1782, consisting of about 36,000 volumes divided into four categories: classics, history, philosophy, and literature. This is the largest book collection in Chinese history. However, during this process, the court also destroyed thousands of books deemed anti-Qing. The Yongle Encyclopedia belongs to the Ming dynasty, while the Taiping Imperial Readings is from the Song dynasty.

cau_hoi: The Chagatai Khanate, one of the khanates of the Mongol Empire, was located in which area?
giai_thich: Chagatai was the second son of Genghis Khan, who was given the territory of Central Asia, which includes most of present-day Uzbekistan, Kazakhstan, and Xinjiang. The Mongol Empire later split into four parts: the Yuan dynasty (China), the Golden Horde (Russia), the Ilkhanate (Persia), and the Chagatai Khanate. Timur originated from this khanate.

cau_hoi: Which Mongol khan died in 1259 while besieging a fortress in Sichuan – Chongqing?
giai_thich: Diao Yu City was a mountain fortress of the Southern Song dynasty, resisting Mongol forces for 36 years. Mongke died during the siege, possibly due to illness or injury. His death forced the Mongol princes to return to fight for the throne, causing the Mongol army advancing into the Middle East to withdraw. Thus, some call this the 'fortress that changed the course of world history.'

cau_hoi: To capture Xiangyang (1268 – 1273), what type of weapon did the Mongol army use?
D: Counterweight trebuchets made by Persian engineers
giai_thich: The Mongol army besieged Xiangyang for nearly 6 years without success. Kublai Khan invited two Muslim engineers from the Ilkhanate in Persia to create counterweight trebuchets, capable of throwing stones weighing dozens of kilograms over great distances. The stones breached the city walls, and Xiangyang surrendered in 1273. This is an example of technology spreading through the Mongol Empire.

cau_hoi: After the Jingkang Incident in 1127, the Song dynasty retreated south and established its capital in which city?
giai_thich: In 1127, the Jurchens (Jin dynasty) captured the capital Bianjing and took both Song emperors captive. A prince escaped south, establishing the Southern Song dynasty and temporarily setting the capital in Lin'an, now known as Hangzhou. 'Lin'an' means 'temporary peace.' Hangzhou, with West Lake, became one of the most beautiful and prosperous cities in the world at that time.

cau_hoi: Which Song general fought against the Jin army and had the four characters 'Loyalty to the Country' inscribed by his mother on his back?
giai_thich: Yue Fei achieved many victories against the Jin army and nearly reclaimed the north. However, Prime Minister Qin Hui, who wanted to negotiate peace, falsely accused him of treason, and Yue Fei was executed in 1142. In front of Yue Fei's tomb in Hangzhou, there is a statue of Qin Hui and his wife kneeling, which has been spat upon by visitors for centuries.

cau_hoi: Which Song chancellor refused to surrender to the Yuan dynasty and left behind the poem 'Song of Righteousness'?
giai_thich: Wen Tianxiang passed the imperial examination and later organized troops to resist the Mongols. Captured in 1278, he was imprisoned in Dadu for over 3 years. Kublai Khan valued his talent and invited him to serve, but he refused and was executed in 1283. The poem 'Song of Righteousness' written in prison became a symbol of loyalty.

cau_hoi: The Western Xia dynasty in northwest China (1038 – 1227) was established by which ethnic group?
giai_thich: The Tangut people established the Western Xia kingdom, which had its own writing system with thousands of complex characters. Western Xia was destroyed by Genghis Khan in 1227, and he also died during this campaign. Subsequently, the culture and writing of Western Xia nearly disappeared, only to be deciphered by scholars in the 20th century.

cau_hoi: The term 'Cathay' that Europeans used to refer to China originated from which ethnic group?
giai_thich: The Khitan established the Liao dynasty (907 – 1125) in northern China and Mongolia. The peoples in Central Asia referred to northern China by their name, and Marco Polo brought the name 'Cathay' back to Europe. To this day, in Russian, China is still called 'Kitai,' which also originates from the name of the Khitan.

cau_hoi: Which dynasty did the famous reform of Prime Minister Wang Anshi take place under?
giai_thich: During the reign of Emperor Shen Zong (11th century), Wang Anshi introduced the "New Laws," such as lending money to farmers at low interest and replacing corvée labor with monetary payments. The reforms faced opposition from conservatives led by historian Sima Qiang, and many policies were abolished after Shen Zong's death. Wang Anshi was also one of the "Eight Great Families of the Tang and Song" in literature.

cau_hoi: The famous scroll painting "Along the River During the Qingming Festival" depicts life in the capital of which dynasty?
giai_thich: The painting by artist Zhang Zeduan is over 5 meters long, depicting the bustling scene in the capital Bianjing (Kaifeng) with over 800 characters, boats, bridges, and shops. This is a valuable source of information about urban life in the 12th century. The painting is now preserved in the Palace Museum in Beijing and is rarely exhibited.

cau_hoi: In 845, which Tang dynasty emperor ordered the suppression of Buddhism, destroying thousands of temples?
giai_thich: Tang Wuzong, who followed Daoism, was concerned about the wealth of Buddhist temples, which did not pay taxes. He ordered the destruction of about 4,600 temples and forced around 260,000 monks and nuns to return to lay life, while confiscating land and bronze statues. Other foreign religions such as Zoroastrianism and Manichaeism were also banned. In contrast, Wu Zetian was a strong supporter of Buddhism.

cau_hoi: What were the Japanese delegations sent to China to learn about culture and political systems during the Tang dynasty called?
giai_thich: From 630 to 894, Japan sent about 15-20 delegations to the Tang dynasty, each consisting of several hundred people, including scholars, monks, and craftsmen. They brought back Chinese characters, Buddhism, laws, and urban planning methods. The sea voyages were very dangerous, with many ships sinking. The poet Abe no Nakamaro stayed in China and served in the Tang court.

cau_hoi: The story of the 47 rōnin (masterless samurai) avenging their lord in 1703 took place during which period of Japanese history?
giai_thich: Lord Asano was forced to commit suicide for drawing his sword to attack official Kira in the Shogun's castle. His samurai waited nearly 2 years before attacking Kira's house and taking his head for revenge. Subsequently, all 46 were captured and ordered to commit suicide. The story became a symbol of loyalty and has been adapted into many plays and films.

cau_hoi: Which emperor built the abandoned capital city of Fatehpur Sikri in India, which was deserted after about 14 years?
giai_thich: Akbar built Fatehpur Sikri ("City of Victory") around 1571 using red sandstone, near the residence of a Sufi saint who predicted the birth of his son. By around 1585, the city was abandoned, possibly due to a lack of water and because the king needed to be closer to the northern border. As a result, the structures have been preserved almost intact.

cau_hoi: Which Mughal emperor had his queen Nur Jahan wielding much of the real power in the court?
giai_thich: Nur Jahan ("Light of the World") was the wife of Emperor Jahangir, the son of Akbar. She issued edicts, minted coins in her name, and even went tiger hunting. Jahangir was addicted to alcohol and opium, allowing her to manage many affairs. Nur Jahan's niece was Mumtaz Mahal, the wife for whom Shah Jahan built the Taj Mahal in memory.

cau_hoi: Which Chola king built the massive Brihadeeswarar temple in Thanjavur in 1010?
giai_thich: Raja Raja I was a great Chola king who expanded his territory into Sri Lanka and the Maldives. The Brihadeeswarar temple, dedicated to the god Shiva, has a tower approximately 66 meters high, with the top stone estimated to weigh around 80 tons. The temple is still worshipped today after more than 1000 years. His son, Rajendra I, was the one who attacked Srivijaya.

cau_hoi: When did the First Anglo-Burmese War begin?
giai_thich: Burma expanded its territory into Assam and Manipur, bordering British India, leading to war (1824-1826). This was one of the most costly wars for the British in India, with many soldiers dying from disease. Burma lost and had to cede Assam, Arakan, and Tenasserim. The subsequent two wars (1852 and 1885) resulted in Burma losing all its territory.

cau_hoi: The Bowring Treaty of 1855, which opened Siam to free trade, was signed with which country?
giai_thich: King Mongkut signed the treaty with John Bowring, the Governor of Hong Kong, representing Britain. Siam reduced import duties to 3% and allowed British citizens to be tried under British law. The treaty caused Siam to lose part of its sovereignty but helped avoid war and opened the way for rice exports. Siam later signed similar treaties with many other countries.
